AYUTTHAYA: Stilt houses in villages north of Bangkok are no longer high enough to stay dry as Thai authorities deliberately flood riverside communities to spare the capital.

Inside the home of Kamonchanok Sathaphonamonwut, raised more than three metres above the ground in Ayutthaya province, her family of three sleeps on makeshift platforms and cannot use the waterlogged toilet.
Her village has been flooded six years in a row, pushing some to move away, while others have raised their houses higher.
"Our area simply cannot cope with this much water anymore," the 34-year-old said, wading through her soaked home.
But while authorities prioritise protecting Bangkok and other business hubs from floods, "when it comes to our residential communities, they neglect us", she said.
Thailand experiences flooding every year during the monsoon season, and scientists say human-made climate change has made heavy rain and floods more frequent and severe.

After devastating floods in 2011, the government expanded embankments, water gates and other infrastructure to direct water away from Bangkok, the historic city of Ayutthaya and industrial zones along the Chao Phraya River, which flows through the capital.

Around 20km from Ayutthaya's centuries-old temple ruins, a Unesco heritage site, residents say floods that once reached their knees now rise above their heads in some areas and can take several months to recede.

Thai irrigation department spokesman Thanet Somboon said climate change, low-lying geography and recently built embankments that altered the natural flow of the Chao Phraya have contributed to more severe flooding of downstream communities.
And after irrigation channels were completely full of diverted water, he said authorities had "no choice but to discharge the remaining water downstream".
As flooding in hard-hit districts has become more severe, many who remain have paid to lift their stilt houses higher and keep their living space dry.

The government's flagship fix is a US$780-million flood diversion canal, designed to carry 1,200 cubic metres of water — around half the volume of an Olympic-size swimming pool — per second around the bottleneck where the Chao Phraya narrows through Ayutthaya.
It is expected to be completed by 2030. — AFP
e1fa23db656a7853: MANCHESTER: Paris Saint-Germain further soured the mood at the Etihad Stadium as Manchester City's first home game since the guilty verdict on widespread flouting of Premier League financial rules ended in a 4-2 Champions League defeat on Wednesday.
The European champions turned on the style to strike three times inside the opening 35 minutes through Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha.
But City stormed back in the second half as Erling Haaland scored twice either side of Maghnes Akliouche's strike that briefly restored PSG's three-goal cushion.
"When you see a game at this level, two teams trying to play football, that was the kind of game we thought it would be," said PSG boss Luis Enrique.
"They created a huge amount of problems for us today. The team that lost today were perhaps a bit unlucky."

The 10-time English champions face swingeing sanctions unless they can successfully appeal the ruling of an independent commission last month, which found the club guilty on over 100 charges of financial impropriety.

City shrugged off the uncertainty over their future to win 3-0 at Liverpool on Sunday and remain top of the Premier League, but PSG showed why they are the favourites to win this competition for a third consecutive season.
"It has been a bit of a strange game because we conceded two goals in two minutes," said City coach Enzo Maresca.
"Second half we did enough to deserve something more."

Former City manager Pep Guardiola returned to the Etihad for the first time since his departure in May, sat behind the club's embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano in a show of solidarity.

City made passing reference to the guilty verdict with a lengthy pre-match video detailing the club's historic moments of celebration both before and after an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 that transformed their fortunes.
Behind one end supporters unravelled a giant banner reading: "I'm City till I die."
Disaster for Donnarumma
Yet the fighting talk in the stands was not matched on the field as City were blown away by a scintillating first 45 minutes from the visitors.
Gianluigi Donnarumma had a point to prove after the Italian goalkeeper was let go by Luis Enrique just months after helping deliver the club's first Champions League title in 2025.
However, it turned out to be a night to forget for the giant Italian.
Donnarumma was caught out at his near post by Doue's effort from outside the box after a lightning counter-attack to open the scoring.
The move for the second goal two minutes later was even more impressive as Doue and Dembele exchanged an elaborate one-two before the latter headed in at the far post.
Achraf Hakimi hit the post before Vitinha rattled in PSG's third from the edge of the box.
Maresca responded with a triple substitution at half-time and managed to salvage some pride, even if the deficit proved too much to overturn.
Antoine Semenyo and Enzo Fernandez missed glaring chances to pull a goal back even before Haaland glanced home a header from Iliman Ndiaye's cross.
Yet, City were hit by a sucker punch when Donnarumma got a hand to Akliouche's effort but the ball looped high into the air and spun back into the net.
Nuno Mendes made a brilliant clearance off his own line and Haaland hit the bar before the Norwegian slotted home his second of the night.
Donnarumma saved a late Ferran Torres penalty to deny the French champions a fifth goal.

But in the battle between two state-backed projects that have reshaped European football, Qatar-owned PSG are the top dogs right now as City face up to a scandal that leaves their litany of trophies over the past 15 years open to question.
PSG go top of the Champions League table after two games with City three points behind in 17th.

a455f9dea90d8fb1: JERUSALEM: The former head of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency on Wednesday sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation weeks before elections in a row over responsibility for Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who polls show in a tight race to stay in power in the Oct 27 election, has been hammered by the opposition for failing to prevent the attack, the deadliest day in Israeli history.

Netanyahu, who has cast himself as a guarantor of Israel's security over his decades-long career, has insisted that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet's then director, Ronen Bar, or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack.
In the 134-page court document, Bar accused Netanyahu of "lying to cover himself" and said it was slanderous to accuse him of "criminal failures" over the attack.
Netanyahu made accusations against Bar "that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of Oct 7", the lawsuit said.
Instead it was Netanyahu's policies over several years that had "increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza", it said.
Bar resigned in June 2025, saying at the time that "all the systems collapsed" in the security agency and that Shin Bet "failed to sound the alarm".
But Bar said he was resigning to take responsibility as head of the organisation and insists he did warn Netanyahu before October 7 of potential threats linked to Hamas.
Bar is seeking three million shekels (around US$968,500) in damages from Netanyahu.
Bar said he telephoned the prime minister's military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack came up but that he did not have Netanyahu's direct number.
"Ronen, are you serious?" Netanyahu responded in a statement issued by his Likud party on Wednesday.
"You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do."
"How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?" he asked.

Hamas stormed into Israel with pickup trucks and paragliders and opened fire at sites including a music festival. The attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally from official Israeli figures, with militants also dragging 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead.

Israel responded with a massive offensive into Gaza that has killed more than 74,300 people, according to the territory's health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable by the UN.
92fcf3f528fff82e: LONDON: Nomadic Ukrainian champions Shakhtar Donetsk celebrated moving into their new Champions League "home" at Stamford Bridge by storming back to beat AEK Athens 3-1 on Wednesday.
Fans of the club turned up in their thousands to support the team, who emerged from the tunnel draped in blue-and-yellow national flags.
The Greek side took the lead in the 28th minute through Lovro Majer but Pedrinho levelled confidently from the penalty spot just six minutes later.
With about 10 minutes of normal time to go, Vinicius Tobias found the net from a tight angle and substitute Gleiker Mendoza made the game safe, smashing home after cutting in from the left.
The result leaves Shakhtar on four points after two games after a draw against PSV Eindhoven in their opening match in the league phase of the Champions League.
Shakhtar, from the east of Ukraine, are using Chelsea's ground as the base for their European fixtures this season, with the Londoners absent from continental competition.
On the eve of the match, the club's chief executive Sergei Palkin spoke of how playing at the home of the two-time European champions would keep the war-torn nation's struggles "visible".
Shakhtar were forced to leave their home ground, the Donbas Arena in Donetsk, after pro-Russia separatists seized control of the city in 2014.
Since then the team has lived an itinerant existence, playing home European matches elsewhere in Ukraine as well in Poland, Germany and Slovenia due to the security situation in their homeland.
London made sense as the next base for the team.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the UK has provided refuge to 265,000 Ukrainians, according to the Ukrainian embassy in London.
Fans from the ex-pat population turned out in force on Wednesday, swelling the crowd to 29,000 - around 11,000 short of capacity.
'Blessing'
"I think it's such a blessing to see my team play here," James Upson, a 20-year-old student, whose mother is from Ukraine and father from the UK, told AFP.
"Obviously, it's unfortunate we can't play in our country, but here it's just a beautiful sight for them to come out to the Champions League anthem in such a beautiful, beautiful stadium."

He said playing in London was a way to keep the Ukraine conflict in the public eye, on a day when Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelensky was in London for talks with British prime minister Andy Burnham.
"We have to keep ourselves relevant, and we do our best to do so," said Upson. "We played in Valencia as the national team recently. You know, we had good outreach there.
"But to have a local club come to the UK and play here in four matches is just such a wonderful sight."
Marta Palas, 17, said many of her classmates do even not realise the war in Ukraine is still going on.
"I'm about to graduate high school and people don't know about the war, at all," she said.
"They think it's not going on anymore, but it does. It's still on, and it does - it did get harsher, honestly, from back in 2022. It is quite a hard situation right now."
Serzh Dadizha, 22, a Ukrainian student who studies in Britain, told AFP he wanted to help his team from the stands.
"I want to feel like I'm a 12th player, like I belong here, like I make an impact for my team, like I do something. Not just to watch the show."
Snoop, who goes by his nickname, travelled all the way London from his home in Finland to watch his adopted team.
"When I was a teenager and I saw what was happening in Donbas and Donetsk, I just felt like some kind of compassion for them," said the 26-year-old. "So yeah, it comes from deep in the heart."
Shakhtar, Uefa Cup winners in 2009 and Conference League semi-finalists last season, next host Sporting Lisbon, with Fenerbahce and Real Madrid to follow at their new temporary home.

MALAYSIAN film industry figures must stop pointing the finger at the audience whenever a movie flops at the box office, said veteran actor and producer Datuk Rosyam Nor.
Instead, the 59-year-old managing director of Suhan Movies and Trading urged filmmakers to look in the mirror and re-examine their production standards, commercial appeal and marketing strategies.
He stressed that viewers are paying customers who deserve well-packaged, high-quality content, no matter the genre.

"Audiences are never in the wrong. They are the buyers. Serve them delicious food beautifully packaged, and buyers will come. Movies work the exact same way," Rosyam remarked during a meet-and-greet session with Anugerah Bintang Popular Berita Harian 2026 nominees at MyKart Raceway in Shah Alam recently.
"Even with epic films, do they possess high commercial value? Are the cast members bankable? Who is steering the ship as director? That is simply the reality of cinema."
The seasoned star noted that only a small fraction of weekly local releases manage to become breakout hits.
"It is not a question of genre, but one of marketing and quality."
To illustrate his point, Rosyam pointed to director Chiu Keng Guan's rally-themed feature 'Terbang'.
He noted that despite Chiu's past success with the blockbuster 'Ola Bola', rally racing has a niche appeal in Malaysia compared to football.
Combined with a lead actor who lacks mass star power, the film faced an uphill struggle at the box office despite its cinematic quality.
Rosyam emphasised that without a proper promotional budget, even solid, well-made films often remain invisible to moviegoers.

3306071a62f4a002: SEOUL: North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries."
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.
Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the Sept 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilised posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.

The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Proven submarine-launched missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, also allowing deployment beyond the Korean peninsula.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, with the latest launches taking place on Monday.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.

ISTANBUL: Barcelona and Lamine Yamal rediscovered their sparkle after a rocky first half in the cauldron of Istanbul's Ali Sami Yen Stadium, winning 4-1 away to Galatasaray in the Champions League on Tuesday.
Yamal tore the hosts apart after half time.
"It's incredible to have players like that," said Barcelona coach Hansi Flick.
"He's turned the game around for us."
Halfway through the second round of matches, the victory lifted Barcelona to the top of the Champions League table with two wins. Galatasaray are pointless and near the foot of the standings.
"We're at a very high level. We have to keep going; the season is very long. We can't relax," said Barcelona's Fermin Lopez.
Barcelona dominated the early stages.
With Yamal vigorously policed on the right by the home defence, many of their attacks flowed through Anthony Gordon on the other flank.
Yet Galatasaray took the lead after 27 minutes.
After Gordon went tumbling in the penalty box, the hosts launched a rapid counter-attack through Rafael Leao.
He pulled the ball back to the edge of the area to Russian Aleksei Batrakov, whose drive deflected off Joao Cancelo and into the corner of the goal.
"That goal made things a bit strange for us, because we had been dominating. But we knew how to react and come back," said Fermin.
The hosts pushed for a second, with Victor Osimhen heading over from a corner and Baris Yilmaz having a goal ruled out for offside.
Barcelona restored parity when Yamal went down on the edge of the area, and Davinson Sanchez gave the ball away.
Dani Olmo fed Cancelo, who finished past the goalkeeper.
Yamal took control in the second half, setting up Fermin to head home a cross in the 50th minute.
Three minutes later, Yamal beat defender Eren Elmali to set up Gordon, who made no mistake from close range.
Yamal then created the fourth goal after 65 minutes, cutting inside to pass to Gabriel Jesus, who laid the ball off for Karim Adeyemi to score. — AFP

835728eef7597788: BODO: Fredrik Sjovold's 52nd-minute strike secured a 1-0 victory for Bodo/Glimt over Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Wednesday, extending the Norwegian side's remarkable home record against Europe's elite.

"Each of us needs to ask ourselves what the problem was," Dortmund captain Waldemar Anton said.

Bodo's run to the round of 16 last season was underpinned by an excellent record at their 8,200-capacity home, officially the smallest venue in this year's competition.
Dortmund arrived in the Arctic Circle on a seven-game unbeaten run but struggled to get a foothold.
The hosts were far more comfortable in the opening half, with Sondre Fet and Ole Blomberg inches away from scoring.
Bodo continued their domination after half-time and broke through when Sjovold turned a low Sondre Auklend cross in at the near post.
Dortmund's level improved after Kovac made four changes on the hour mark, with substitute Nmecha forcing a fingertip save from goalkeeper Nikita Haikin moments later.
The Germans upped the pressure in the dying stages but failed to find a way through as they fell to a first defeat this campaign since the season-opening German Super Cup.
0f57e5555edae0cb: SAN FRANCISCO: Netflix is laying off 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 employees, in its biggest cuts since 2022, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters, as the streaming pioneer faces tough competition for viewers from legacy rivals and YouTube.
The bulk of the job cuts would be in Netflix's product, tech, legal and human-resources teams, the email Co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos sent to employees on Wednesday showed.
"Our mission -- to entertain the world -- is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources," they said in the memo.
"Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast."
Netflix shares, down around 25% so far this year, rose 0.7% on Wednesday. The company had about 16,000 employees at the end of last year.
This year, the streaming giant has faced doubts about its ability to sustain the growth that disrupted the US media industry by putting pressure on cable TV businesses.

Engagement, or the amount of time users spend on Netflix, has become a key concern for investors as platforms such as YouTube and TikTok attract viewers with free-to-watch, user-generated content that gives them a cost advantage over Netflix.

A failed pursuit of Warner Bros Discovery's streaming and studio assets earlier this year deepened doubts about Netflix's strategy. Paramount completed its US$110-billion Warner Bros acquisition earlier this month to form Skydance.

"They haven't been able to find like another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer, adding the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a ceiling.
"Eventually, because they've kind of nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle."
Netflix has been trying to expand beyond its subscription business by investing in ad tiers, live programming and gaming.
Its last major round of layoffs came in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs in two rounds after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday's memo.

17d737eeadde1515: ROME: Jose Mourinho enjoyed a Roma reunion to remember as Real Madrid completed an astonishing comeback by scoring three late goals to claim a 4-3 away win in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Marten de Roon gave the hosts a deserved opener before Kylian Mbappe struck back on his 100th Champions League appearance to level the scores at the break.
Two Donyell Malen strikes in the space of six minutes early in the second half seemed to take the game away from the 15-time European champions as Roma ran rampant.

But Real scored three goals in the final six minutes, all stemming from corners, to turn the game on its head as Carlos Espi, Endrick and ex-Roma defender Antonio Rudiger struck at a stunned Stadio Olimpico.
Mourinho was a popular figure as he led Roma to the Uefa Conference League title and Europa League final during two-and-a-half years in charge.

The Portuguese was honoured with banners and chants by the home crowd in Roma's first home Champions League match in more than seven years, and the hosts started strongly as Mario Hermoso forced Thibaut Courtois into a flying fingertip save.

Roma took a deserved lead when De Roon swept a shot past Courtois from 25 yards in the 20th minute, and almost doubled it when Malen's powerful shot squirmed under Courtois before being plucked off the line.
However, one costly moment of switching off proved enough to send them back to square one within five minutes of the opener being scored.

Hermoso misjudged an interception to allow Mbappe a clear run at goal and the France striker's deflected shot flew into the roof of the net to level the scores with Real's first meaningful chance of the game.

Mbappe marked his Champions League centurion status, something he is the youngest player to achieve aged 27, with his 72nd tournament goal – one that moved him into the all-time top five ahead of Real legend Raul Gonzalez.
The equaliser appeared to subdue Roma and steady Mourinho's men, who twice threatened a second before the break as Marc Cucurella and Jude Bellingham came close.

But Roma boss Gian Piero Gasperini insisted pre-match that Roma would not compromise on their full-throttle style regardless of opposition, and he was true to his word as they came out firing after the break.

Roma quickly re-took the lead when half-time substitute Rodrigo Mora fed the ball to Malen, who finished brilliantly by taking the ball in his stride with his first touch and lifting it over Courtois with his second.
Things got even better for the Italians just six minutes later when Malen raced onto a through ball to power home his second, given following a VAR review after initially being flagged for offside.
Real looked for a response as Mbappe twice tested Pierluigi Gollini, before having his second goal of the night ruled out for offside.

But set-pieces proved to be the key to unlock the Roma defence, as Espi tucked home a close-range rebound from a header to pull one back before Endrick powered home a header from another corner just two minutes later.
The final blow was struck by Rudiger in the 90th minute, the defender getting in front of his marker to guide home a close-range finish and complete an extraordinary turnaround.
The result leaves Real Madrid with six points from their opening two league phase matches, while Roma are on one point.

fe92b14a894135d4: NEW YORK: Hotter-than-expected inflation data sent the Nasdaq to a sharply lower close on Wednesday, with worries about more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve pummeling shares of Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs.

Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise sank 11.4% and 8.2%, respectively, after Barclays downgraded the AI server makers to "equal-weight" from "overweight".

Apple rose 0.5%, with its market capitalisation closing above US$5 trillion for the first time.
US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged and price pressures broadened beyond energy, data from the labor department's Bureau of Labor Statistics showed.
Interest-rate traders are pricing in a 37% chance that Fed policymakers will raise rates this month, up from 22% on Tuesday, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"Investors are not happy with the report because that puts pressure on the Fed to raise rates to combat inflation," said Adam Sarhan, chief executive of 50 Park Investments, in New York. "Inflation remains public enemy number one for the market and for the Fed."
The S&P 500 declined 1.11% to end the session at 7,718.94 points, its biggest one-day drop since July 29.

Volume on US exchanges was relatively heavy, with 18.0 billion shares traded, compared to an average of 17.6 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions.

After hitting a record high last week, the S&P 500 remains up almost 13% in 2026, with most of that gain fueled by AI-related stocks. The median S&P 500 stock has gained 4% in 2026, and over 200 of the index's components are in negative territory.

The S&P 500 Banks index dipped 0.7% to its lowest close since June.

Before the inflation data was released, Fed vice-chair for supervision Michelle Bowman said the central bank had time to wait and see how markets and the economy evolve after its September rate rise before deciding further action.
Bending Spoons rallied 41% after Berkshire Hathaway invested another US$330 million in the owner of Vimeo and AOL, a big endorsement from the high-profile investor whose moves traders closely follow.
Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.1-to-one ratio.

5032509adc3ae559: ISTANBUL: Police raided Turkey's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, early Wednesday, halting broadcasts and installing a government-appointed administrator in the latest move against pro-opposition media.
They also raided homes, arresting 11 people -- among them a journalist and seven family members of Halk TV chairman Cafer Mahiroglu, who described it as "a dark day for Turkey".
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," Halk wrote on X as its live news channel and YouTube broadcasts were cut during the pre-dawn raids.

It was the latest move against media viewed as critical of Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government, coming two weeks after officials closed the website and social media accounts of leading digital news website T24, citing "LGBT propaganda".

Prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of a probe into Mahiroglu on suspicion of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering. They confirmed seizing companies co-owned or managed by him with trustees placed at the helm.
But Mahiroglu said the allegations were "baseless" and accused the government of using the judiciary for political ends.

"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," he said in a video on X, confirming seven family members had been detained including his 70-year-old brother. He himself is also named in the warrant but lives abroad.
"Using the judiciary as a weapon is the greatest harm inflicted on Turkey," he said. "We will get our channel back."
'Brutal blow'
As dawn broke, staff and journalists gathered in the pouring rain outside the headquarters where hundreds of riot police stood behind shields outside the building, an AFP correspondent said.
Staff were later allowed in.
Footage of the moment when the feed was cut showed a live interview about a huge investment-fund scandal suddenly switching to a classic film from 1973.

29ad242422527ec3: Despite previous controversies, it seems like the lords of Linux are warming to AI-assisted coding. The penguin's kernel community has agreed to stop asking coders to disclose whether they used bots to help with their contributions. And Linux kernel supremo Linus Torvalds has made clear that he opposes "stupid" AI disclosure rules as long as people understand the code they're submitting. "The Maintainers Summit reached consensus to deprecate the Assisted-by Tag," said Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer and engineer at Nvidia, in a message to the Linux kernel mailing list last week. "Remove the documentation requiring it." The policy had said that those using "any sort of advanced coding tool in the creation of [their] patch" should acknowledge that through the addition of an "Assisted-by" tag in the commit message. The AI labeling proposal initially took shape in July 2025. It became part of the documentation in January 2026. This was shortly after Torvalds said that he was fairly positive about vibe coding as a way for people to get into programming, but remained skeptical about its effect on software maintainability. Since then, he's warmed to AI tool usage. AI attribution wasn't an issue when the generated code was obvious, buggy, and bad. But in the past year or so, AI coding agents started producing code that is of acceptable quality for the purposes of the Linux kernel community. "LLMs are good enough now," said Greg Kroah-Hartman, a veteran Linux kernel maintainer, at the Linux Foundation's Open Source Summit in South Korea in August. "They've gotten good enough to find bugs because LLMs, AI, are just pattern matchers and code is nothing but patterns in a specific format." Cautious acceptance hasn't erased concerns about errors slipping through unnoticed, accountability, and coding agents reproducing copyrighted code. There's also still a stigma in some circles around the use of AI tools. Those who have spent years honing software skills, coding with limited assistance from tools, may disparage developers who don't understand the code they conjure with a prompt. Rapid change will do that – in the space of a few years, software production practices have changed drastically, and software quality, security, and maintenance practices have yet to fully adjust. The leading makers of AI coding agents – Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and the like – are doing their best to promote AI-driven projects as better than anything a human developer could manage. Yet even they differ in their AI attribution practices. Claude adds provenance messages by default, but Codex does not. In fields such as advertising and art, content provenance can help assess misinformation and human creative input. For code, the focus tends to be more on functionality than form. In a prior discussion of the merits of the tag requirement, Jeff Layton, a Linux kernel developer with Red Hat, explained the rationale for reversing course. First, he said, not everyone abides by the policy. Second, he said, "it basically serves as free advertising for proprietary LLM companies." And third, he said, "it's not clear why we want to collect this info in the first place." Some kernel contributors still see value in the tagging requirement. "I'm not happy removing the tag without adding another mechanism for required disclosure," said Laurent Pinchart, a Linux kernel dev and founder of Ideas on Board, in a mailing list post on Tuesday. "Without that, I can foresee submitters pushing back on the question." Pinchart challenged the argument that AI labeling rules will just be ignored. "What this is about is setting our expectations, telling what we want and what we don't want," said Pinchart. "There's still value in that, and I'd argue there's even more value now. There will be people who won't care, there will be people who cheat. We've always had those, we'll keep having them, and we'll keep rejecting their contributions. I really don't get the unenforceable argument here." Linus Torvalds responded with an emphatic rejection of tool usage declarations. He wrote: What you are about is something entirely different. It has nothing to do with "expectations", and it has everything to do with your hangups. I don't understand this whole idiotic concept of "don't use AI for X". Here's a new rule just for you: don't use compilers for any of your kernel submissions. Because if you can't show that you really understand what the machine is actually doing by writing your code in assembler, then I don't want to see your code contribution. You clearly aren't competent if you can't write it that way. And btw, you had better not use an editor to write that commit message either. Because I need you to show me that you can actually write a good commit message without using tools that make it easy to backspace and hide the mistakes you made while typing. Ok? Because otherwise those tool-assisted commits of yours clearly aren't showing that you know what you are doing. Do you not see how UTTERLY STUPID those kinds of rules would be? So no. We're not going to make stupid rules that say "you can't use tools for X". The kind of expectations *I* have is that people do their best and I expect people to understand what they are doing. But that understanding has very little to do with what tools they use. And quite honestly, in my experience, the people I respect and call intelligent are not the ones that shy away from using new and interesting tools. ®

15182b3efcde6535: Researchers at security startup Xbow used OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model to help chain three zero-day vulnerabilities in Chrome into an exploit capable of executing code outside the browser's sandbox on Windows machines. Xbow estimates that this could affect about one billion users worldwide. Google fixed all three, and paid the Xbow team a $250,000 bounty, its top reward for a Chrome full-chain exploit. The payout also proves a nice return on investment for the human bug hunters - Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers - who spent just six days during the Black Hat and DEF CON conferences and about $40,000 in token charges to discover the vulnerabilities and build the attack chain. “The number on the check is impressive, but the time it took our team, with the help of a publicly available AI model, to break in is even more impressive,” Xbow CEO and founder Oege de Moor said on Tuesday. “A three letter intelligence-agency veteran told me that his team used to spend six months trying to identify this kind of vulnerability and get total access. We did it in six days.” In a separate technical writeup about the attack chain, Dolan-Gavitt detailed the work done by humans and AI agents. Agents, using OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol model, searched source code, tested the team’s hypotheses, and developed proofs of concept and exploit stages, he said. Meanwhile, the AI pen-testing security startup’s researchers chose targets, provided context, challenged the agents’ results, and decided which attack components to chain. "We did apply a fair bit of our own human expertise and judgment," he wrote. Crossing two security boundaries in 3 steps Google’s Chrome browser uses several layers of security to protect users, and this includes sandboxes - barriers to contain compromised code and ensure that someone who hacks an individual website can’t take over the entire computer. This includes deploying the V8 sandbox to prevent any memory corruption flaws in the V8 JavaScript engine from impacting other memory. The V8 sandbox sits inside the operating-system process sandbox, and this nested design means that escaping V8's memory restrictions doesn't automatically grant native code execution. Even if an attacker achieves native code execution inside Chrome's renderer, the outer process sandbox restricts access to the rest of the machine. “The chain crossed both boundaries in three vulnerability stages,” abusing Chrome to run code on Windows machines, Dolan-Gavitt wrote. The attack combines a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad. The first vulnerability is in Maglev, V8's mid-tier optimizing compiler, and it’s due to a reused, mutable boxed number during deoptimization. This gives attackers read and write access throughout V8's pointer-compression cage. The second stage, the animated-WebP bug, is a V8 sandbox escape. “But rather than attacking the sandbox itself we exploited a property that the V8 sandbox deliberately does not enforce and that Blink incorrectly assumed it could trust,” Dolan-Gavitt explained. “Finally, the exploit used an overflow in Crashpad to cross the final outer process boundary and achieve unsandboxed code execution on the host.” While Google patched all three security issues, and Chrome installs updates on its own, a fix only takes effect once the user relaunches the browser. If you use Chrome, make sure you are running version 152.0.7977.82 or later. The time and money spent to achieve a full chain Chrome exploit illustrate - yet again - that “the bar is significantly lower” for attackers armed with LLMs, Dolan-Gavitt wrote. “Defend accordingly.”®

972ce96df38a5766: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.

Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.

The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)
7f9bbf2a1cbccf2f: IN October 2024, a federal jury in Las Vegas convicted Michele Fiore, a local elected official and ardent supporter of President Donald Trump, of charity fraud.
Fiore, the jury found, solicited donations for a slain police officer's memorial and spent nearly US$80,000 of it on plastic surgery, her daughter's wedding and rent.
The jury deliberated for less than two hours, including a lunch break, before finding Fiore guilty on seven charges brought by the Department of Justice.

Weeks before she was to be sentenced last year, Trump granted Fiore "a full and unconditional pardon," sparing her the prospect of decades in prison, payment of criminal fines, and any restitution to donors whose funds she misspent.

In a statement at the time, a White House spokesperson noted Fiore's support for the president and said that Biden-era prosecutors had targeted the politician, known in Nevada as "Lady Trump," because of "outspoken conservative views."
In an email to Reuters, Fiore criticized prosecutors and witnesses and maintained her innocence.
"I have never taken one red cent of donations for my personal use," she wrote. She declined to answer detailed questions about her career, case and conviction.

Fiore is one of at least 85 public officials granted clemency by Trump after charges or convictions related to corruption, according to the first comprehensive examination of such measures over the president's two terms in office so far.

The Reuters review shows that the political impetus behind Fiore's pardon wasn't an outlier: The recipients of Trump's clemency for public officials overwhelmingly have been fellow Republicans or vocal proponents of his MAGA movement.
They include at least 11 of 15 Republican members of Congress convicted of wrongdoing over the past two decades.
Of the 85 public officials identified in Reuters' analysis, 36 were elected as Republicans and another 19 were Republicans appointed to political office.

Nine others had either campaigned for Trump or publicly espoused support for his agenda. Only four were known Democrats, including one Texas congressman whom Trump erroneously believed would switch parties after the pardon.
The news agency couldn't determine partisan affiliation for the 17 other officials.

Trump's repeated acts of clemency for public officials charged with or convicted of corruption-related crimes have led to what more than a dozen current and former prosecutors, along with other legal experts and political researchers, say is impunity for people meant to uphold the public trust.
The impunity, these people said, can encourage more wrongdoing by other officials, eroding the foundational democratic concept that no one, no matter what office they hold, is above the law.
The problem, they added, is compounded if the concept of clemency is tainted by perceptions of partisan or personal bias.

"President Trump is trying to end accountability for public officials," said Phillip Halpern, a retired assistant US attorney in San Diego who prosecuted two Republican congressmen Trump later pardoned.
"He's setting a standard to encourage corruption and allow it to flourish."

Trump's absolution has allowed nearly three-quarters of the 85 officials in Reuters' analysis to leave prison early, evade trials or sentencing, or regain eligibility to exercise certain freedoms, like owning a gun.
In total, the analysis found, these people were spared 130 years behind bars and avoided payment of more than US$15 million in financial penalties.

More than half of the recipients have remained in politics either as public officials or as vocal supporters of Trump and his agenda. That includes Fiore, who isn't working but is still earning a government salary as a Nevada county justice of the peace.

Noting his own indictments by federal prosecutors during the presidency of Joe Biden, Trump has said he aims to right wrongs by a DOJ that he has claimed – repeatedly and without evidence – targeted innocent people for partisan purposes.
"I am your warrior," he told a conservative gathering in 2023, while campaigning for re-election. "I am your justice. And for those who have been wronged and betrayed, I am your retribution."
Administration officials have repeatedly defended the president's use of the pardon power, granted by the Constitution and ample in scope.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, in a statement said Trump grants clemency for "many Americans unjustly prosecuted by the Biden administration's weaponised Department of Justice."
Reuters' review encompassed clemency recipients who held an elected or appointed government role or were employed in the civil or uniformed services.
Most were paid from government coffers. Recipients included seven advisors to Trump, three DOJ officials, three governors, 10 state lawmakers, two city council members, two judges and two sheriffs.
Their charges and crimes included fraud, bribery, conspiracy, racketeering, obstruction of justice and others.

Reuters' tally of public officials doesn't include at least 18 active-duty military, police and government employees who were among those charged with or convicted for storming the US Capitol on Jan 6, 2021.

Before Trump issued his blanket clemency for the roughly 1,500 people involved in the riot, many of these 18 had used their official credentials to rally others against the peaceful transfer of power after the 2020 election.
Some of Trump's predecessors have also drawn fire for controversial use of the pardon power, most recently Biden because of clemency for his son, Hunter, convicted on federal gun and tax charges.
Both Biden and former President Barack Obama commuted more prison sentences than Trump, cutting short the punishments of many non-violent drug offenders.
But over his nearly six years in office so far, Trump has granted far more pardons than any other recent president, particularly through his mass clemency for the Capitol rioters.
SENDING SIGNALS
Earlier this year, Reuters examined the president's upending of the pardon process.
In nearly 2,000 acts of clemency, Trump has forgone longstanding practice of presidents working with the DOJ to evaluate who should merit clemency.
He has instead relied on a growing number of clemency consultants who, leveraging close ties to the president or his inner circle, advocate for would-be recipients.

The shift, the news agency found, has marginalised the DOJ, where a series of guidelines shaped the process for more than a century and sought to ensure that recipients admit guilt and espouse remorse before receiving clemency.

Among many of those whom Trump pardoned, Reuters found, remorse has mostly been replaced by defiance, expressions of disdain for prosecutors and courts, and a sense of victimisation similar to that voiced by the president himself.
Of the 85 public officials in the Reuters review, more than three-quarters didn't cooperate with prosecutors.
Most neither pleaded guilty nor publicly expressed remorse after their conviction.
Trump's repeated pardoning of public officials, legal experts say, is part of a broader weakening of the federal government's tools to fight corruption in the first place.

Consider the administration's management of the DOJ's Public Integrity Section, a prosecutorial office established after the Watergate crisis to fight corruption and prevent the politicisation of criminal cases.
More than half of the public officials in Reuters' review were charged or convicted in cases prosecuted with involvement by the Public Integrity Section.

That team, based in Washington, numbered about 30 at the end of the Biden administration. The squad now has just two full-time prosecutors, according to four people familiar with the office's operations.
In addition to several senior prosecutors in the unit who resigned in protest of new department directives, others moved elsewhere in the DOJ.

Audrey Cook, a DOJ spokesperson, in a statement wrote that the department "remains committed to identifying, investigating, and prosecuting public corruption wherever the facts and the law warrant it."
She added: "No one should mistake the President's use of his constitutional pardon authority for a change in the law or a license to engage in criminal conduct."

At the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which historically worked closely with the Public Integrity Section, Director Kash Patel last year shut down an elite squad that focused on corruption and fired some of its investigators.
Patel claimed the squad, known as CR-15, was "weaponising law enforcement" in its investigation of false claims by Trump and Republican lawmakers that Biden stole the 2020 presidential election.
FBI officials didn't respond to requests from Reuters for comment.
Changes like those to the Public Integrity Section have slowed prosecution of corruption cases.

The DOJ generally charges hundreds of federal, state and local officials with corruption-related crimes annually, according to summaries the DOJ provided to Congress each year before Trump resumed office in 2025.

But so far in his second term, the DOJ hasn't disclosed the start of a single new bribery case, according to a June study authored by two former anti-corruption prosecutors and published by the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law.

"Why would any prosecutor or FBI agent want to do this kind of work now?" said Molly Gaston, one of the authors and one of several DOJ veterans fired by the administration because of their involvement in Trump's prosecution.
"It's nothing but a career killer."
For those convicted before the recent pullback in prosecution, Trump's pardons can be career revivers.
And for Trump, the pardons can generate goodwill that the recipients then redeploy on behalf of the president and his agenda.

"If President Trump asks me to do just about anything, I'll do it," said Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor, a Democrat, who was convicted last decade for crimes including his effort to sell Obama's vacant Senate seat.

Since leaving prison, and receiving a commutation and pardon from Trump, Blagojevich has reemerged as a lobbyist, earning US$50,000 this year for helping a fugitive former Indiana city councilman seek a pardon, federal lobbying records show.
He is also busy promoting a forthcoming book, "Framed, F*cked, and Freed," relating his legal travails and featuring a blurb from Trump calling Blagojevich's conviction "a terrible injustice."
Blagojevich told Reuters that Trump, during a phone call after his pardon in 2025, said he would support a political comeback for the former governor.
Reuters couldn't independently confirm the details of the conversation.

"The signal he sends with the pardon power is: If you help me personally, Donald Trump, I will help you personally, even if you engaged in corruption," said Rachel Barkow, a New York University law professor and clemency expert.
"A HIGHER STANDARD"

Some of Trump's pardons, including Fiore's, have prompted outrage from pro-Trump partisans. Before Trump pardoned him last year, John Rowland, a Connecticut Republican who served as a state lawmaker, congressman and governor, had a rap sheet as a repeat offender.

In 2004, he pleaded guilty and served 10 months in prison for accepting illegal gifts as governor. A decade later, he was sentenced to 30 months in prison for concealing payments for consulting he had done on behalf of congressional candidates.
That conviction included charges of conspiracy and falsification of records.

"He obviously didn't learn his lesson," said Christopher Shays, a former Republican congressman who represented Connecticut for over two decades, overlapping with much of Rowland's time in Congress and the governor's mansion.
"If you have public officials who believe they can get away with being corrupt, there will be more corruption."
When Trump pardoned Rowland in May of last year, neither the president nor the White House gave a reason for the clemency or commented on it publicly.
Rowland, in a statement at the time, expressed gratitude but didn't detail the process that led to it. In an email to Reuters, he declined to comment further.
As with the many others granted clemency by Trump, the paths to pardons for some public officials lay through well-connected advocates who have no ties to law or criminal justice.

A Tennessee lawmaker and one of his aides, for instance, was each sentenced last year to more than two years in prison and fines of more than US$20,000 for a bribery and kickback scheme using taxpayer money.
Trump gave them full pardons after a country singer vouched on their behalf.

In 2019, local press reported that Cade Cothren, then an aide to the speaker of the lower house of the Tennessee legislature, had texted profane and racist messages to his boss and others, and said he used cocaine in the General Assembly building.
Cothren resigned as a result, and Glen Casada, the speaker, relinquished his post but served out his term as a legislator.

ceb6a0020de2d9e5: It's about time: the General Conference on Weights and Measures looks set to end leap seconds in an effort to reach horological harmony. Since 1972, 27 leap seconds have been added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to keep it in step with the astronomical time scale UT1, which is based on Earth's fluctuating rotation. The proposal would increase the permitted difference between UTC and UT1 from 0.9 seconds to one hour, avoiding leap-second adjustments for centuries. Earth's rotation has also sped up in recent years, raising the possibility of a negative leap second – removing a second rather than adding one. That has never been done before. Experts have estimated a 30 percent probability that global systems will need a negative leap second by 2035 to keep the two time measures in step. That could pose problems for computer systems designed to handle added seconds but not removed ones. Many national bodies support the proposal, which is expected to pass. If approved, the change would take effect on May 20, 2027. Setnam Shemar, principal scientist at the UK's National Physical Laboratory, said the proposal would avoid the risks associated with leap seconds for centuries. "Leap seconds can be difficult to implement reliably, and if not applied correctly, they can cause differences in time across networks, potentially leading to the failure of systems such as mobile phone networks or electricity grids. These risks could increase if a negative leap second had to be implemented for the first time. "Previously, leap seconds were added to UTC to keep it within 0.9 seconds of UT1. From 20 May 2027, a difference of up to 1 hour will be allowed before intervention is needed, ensuring the continuity of UTC for several centuries or more. "The relationship between UTC and UT1 is important for some applications, such as astronomy and celestial navigation. The decision would not sever that link: UT1 will continue to be monitored, and its difference from UTC will continue to be disseminated through established international services." ®
88d33e11bddc035f: Silicon Valley’s AI bros have supposedly found a new way to signal to those around them how committed they are to their industry: Take up smoking despite the risk of cancer, because they expect bots to develop a cure … any day now. At least, that’s the claim Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar made in a recent interview on CBS's Face the Nation. In trying to explain what he described as a doomsday cult surrounding effective altruism, whose adherents include some AI researchers who believe the technology could bring about a utopia, Sankar claimed smoking has become a way for researchers to demonstrate their faith in the tech. “So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI,” Sankar said to the confusion of host Margaret Brennan. Those researchers “believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer, I'm showing you my chips are all in,” Sankar explained. Sankar described the decision to take up smoking as a bet that AI would cure any health ailments that arose from it as “mass psychosis” and “social delusion” that’s getting in the way of actual discussions around the state of AI, and he blamed Silicon Valley’s pet philosophy, effective altruism, for those delusions. “There's an unseen force driving the narrative around AI safety, and it's really this millenarian doomsday cult meets messianic complex called effective altruism,” Sankar said. That philosophy prioritizes making the most effective decisions that benefit the most humans – like utilitarianism on steroids – and it tends to take a long-term approach to things. That’s where AI comes in: Effective altruists are ostensibly focused on ensuring AI systems are built in a way that will best benefit humanity. That focus has been a key reason why so much AI doomerism has come out of Silicon Valley too: If we’re going to build safe AI, says the effective altruist, we have to make sure that we consider all the risks. “There's only really roughly 2,000 AI researchers in America, and the vast majority of them believe in this sort of worldview around effective altruism,” Sankar noted. The Palantir CTO seems to believe, like many effective altruism critics, that all the doomsday scenarios and far-fetched risks being posited by the EA AI crowd are less technical critiques and more like theological ones. “I think there's a profound truth to Pascal's saying that every human has a god-shaped hole in their heart,” Sankar said, “and it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI.” Smoking as a bet that the machine god will save them from cancer, therefore, is akin to the ascetic’s endurance of physical pain or trauma in the hopes God will heal them or see them safely through their torment. From a more practical perspective, this isn’t exactly a great idea, as one former cancer researcher who spoke to The Register told us. “Good luck to them with this approach,” the researcher, who declined to be named, opined. “Even more so, good luck to their non-smoking friends and family taking in their passive smoke.” Taking up smoking in the hopes of a cure may not be a wise idea when one considers the timeline needed to develop a cancer drug, much less a cancer cure. "Even with AI, developing and introducing a new cancer drug into any of the world's health systems can take several years,” the researcher explained. “Even then we wouldn't know whether or not resistance to the drug would develop in the tumors.” The ability of AI to discover drugs and medical treatments has been much hyped – Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis even predicted last year that 2025 would be the year humans started popping AI-designed pills. That hasn’t happened yet, and there’s no real indication it will anytime soon. In other words, the likelihood that AI is going to kill us all is ridiculously overblown. The actual casualties, it seems, are more likely to be the AI bros giving themselves cancer as a show of faith in their machine god. ®

a74c6af825f02775: SOUTH Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after the North announced the artificial intelligence-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Hypersonics are defined as being able to travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound — Mach 5, or more than 6,100 kilometres per hour.
By cutting flight times, they also reduce the opportunity to respond.
They can be capable of carrying conventional or nuclear warheads, depending on the design, and have the potential to alter the strategic balance.
Hypersonic glide vehicles, like those tested by South Korea, are launched into the upper atmosphere by rocket boosters or ballistic missiles before gliding towards their targets.
In addition to their sheer speed, hypersonic missiles can manoeuvre in mid-flight.
Their ability to weave, dip and change course as they descend towards their targets makes them harder to track and intercept than conventional ballistic missiles.

Existing missile defence systems are "better equipped to intercept conventional ballistic and cruise missiles, while hypersonic weapons — along with drones for different reasons — remain particularly challenging threats", said Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs.
That makes them harder for ground-based radar systems to detect until they are closer to their targets.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw the launch of a hypersonic missile that allegedly used AI, state media reported this month.
Pyongyang has said there was "no way to avoid" the missile that was "capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude".
It also said that the missile's "wave-like trajectory mode" left South Korea and Japan unable to track it effectively.
Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification said the launch was "more than a display of individual weapons, but a demonstration of an entire range of missile systems".
"It sends a signal that North Korea has weapons capable of evading interception across different ranges."

But the nuclear-armed North is still believed to remain relatively weak in the critical technology needed to manoeuvre hypersonic missiles in the final stages of flight while maintaining strike accuracy, said the Korea Institute for Military Affairs' Hong Sung-pyo.
"My understanding is that North Korea is now conducting test launches aimed at perfecting that capability, with technological assistance from Russia."
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, calling it a "key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield".
The test assessed heat-resistant materials, guidance and control systems, and the weapon's ability to manoeuvre at low altitudes at hypersonic speeds.

Its "unpredictable flight trajectories and overwhelming speed" could enable strikes on key strategic targets and provide a new deterrence capability on the Korean Peninsula, the presidential Blue House said.
The decision for Seoul to publicly disclose the test was also a political one, said Jung Heon-joo, a public policy professor at Yonsei University in Seoul.
"Possessing this hypersonic technology could signal to potential adversaries that South Korea has a range of weapons options and that attacking it would not be easy."
There were "multiple audiences (for the test launch) — North Korea, the South Korean public and neighbouring countries", he said.

North Korea also fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast on Monday, with experts saying the mixed launches may have been intended to complicate the ability of South Korean and US defence systems to respond.

"The purpose of mixing different types of ballistic missiles is to neutralise South Korean and US missile defence systems," said Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, adding that the launches appeared focused on operational training rather than testing new weapons.

The two Koreas' pursuit of hypersonic weapons could further fuel an arms race on the peninsula, while their speed and manoeuvrability could make detection and interception harder, with implications for US and Japanese defences, analysts say.
"The continued development of advanced weapons systems by both Koreas could intensify the arms race and further entrench the 'two hostile states' framework", Yang said.

8680dd42442948f6: UNITED States President Donald Trump's trademark ability to talk down oil markets with a few words is fading as the Iran war drags on, leaving global energy prices far more exposed to escalation.
The Republican president's so-called "jawboning" was one of the defining features of the Iran conflict's early months after fighting erupted in late February.

In the months before the short-lived July ceasefire, Trump's repeated public statements and social media posts that said Washington and Teheran were edging towards a deal to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz helped keep oil prices well below record highs.
That rhetoric appeared to work even as the blockage of the chokepoint, which previously handled about a fifth of global oil supplies, upended energy markets.
Trump repeatedly predicted during the months of Israeli-US airstrikes that oil prices would "drop like a rock" once a ceasefire deal with Iran is reached.

Traders likely deemed it too risky to bet against Trump's desire to avoid a domestic fuel price spike. As stockpiles deteriorated, they assumed the US president would pull back and end the war quickly.
That bet appeared to pay off until markets learned the limitations of Trump's control.

The July ceasefire broke down, giving way to a protracted, low-level conflict that has spread throughout the region, including the recent escalation in violence between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
This lack of market confidence is now undermining the president's efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices, a key priority before US midterm elections that are only three weeks away.
For energy markets, the era of the Trump trade may be over.
Global benchmark Brent crude prices have held stubbornly above US$100 a barrel for most of the past few weeks, despite a strong recovery in oil flows through Hormuz.
Crude exports through the critical waterway have rebounded to roughly 80 to 90 per cent of pre-war levels.
Yet repeated efforts by Trump and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright to calm markets by highlighting the recovery in flows have not proven effective.
The Trump administration can't "talk" those realities away anymore.
It turns out that increasing flows is one thing. Convincing traders that supplies will remain secure is much harder.
Nowhere is that more evident than in the diesel market.

The combined impact of the Middle East conflict and Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian energy infrastructure has sharply reduced global refining capacity, limiting gasoline, diesel and jet fuel output.

US diesel prices have climbed to fresh records of US$6.50 a gallon, while US gasoline prices remain elevated, worsening a cost-of-living squeeze that has become a major political challenge for Trump ahead of the Nov 3 elections.
It is, therefore, no surprise that the administration has spent much of the past few weeks searching for ways to cool the diesel market.
Trump last week announced an agreement with President Vladimir Putin under which Russia would resume some diesel exports to ease the global shortage.

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct 9.

But the volumes involved are modest. The total promised Russian exports over the next three months amount to around 15 million barrels, equivalent to only about half of one day's global diesel consumption.
Trump also announced on Sunday an energy infrastructure ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, although neither side has publicly confirmed adherence to the agreement.

Yet so far, Trump's "diesel diplomacy" has had only a limited effect. US wholesale diesel prices were flat on Monday, European diesel futures dropped two per cent while Brent rose around two per cent to nearly US$107 a barrel.

The loss of around two million barrels per day of refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East, and the sharp drawdown in global oil inventories have left energy markets in a precarious position that cannot be fixed through rhetoric or relatively small supply additions.
Markets simply don't believe Trump has the ability to bring about a resolution.
The president can still move energy markets with his words, but that power has clearly weakened as the web of conflicts has become more complicated.
The writer is from Reuters

339aa8baab926568: A browser-based emulator for the original iPhone is the latest project to tap into the rich vein of nostalgia running through the tech industry. While far from a complete implementation, the emulation does enough to evoke happier times, before Apple burdened its mobile operating system with frills and complexities, and spent years (and multiple operating system updates) making the Podcasts app steadily more broken. The browser-based emulation (and we use the term carefully; anyone expecting all the functionality of yesteryear will be sorely disappointed) shows an original iPhone as it debuted in 2007. The buttons are where you remember them, the screen is ringed by bezels that wouldn't pass muster today, and the skeuomorphic icons are all present and correct. There's even the browser, though it doesn't do much yet. Even a gentle prod shows how incomplete this implementation is. Some apps work well, such as Calculator, while others - Contacts - struggle, and anything that needs an online connection fails, including loading today's web in 2007's Safari. It does, however, recall how simple things were almost 20 years ago, when the iPhone first appeared, and it joins an array of old-time systems that can be fired up (or at least look like they are) in a browser. Want a look at Apple's abandoned System 7 replacement? Step this way. Perhaps an XP-like implementation? No problem. It would be churlish to dwell on the emulation's deficiencies. For now, it's arguably more curiosity than anything else: Apple didn't launch the App Store until 2008, so third-party apps would be off the table, at least until a later version of iOS landed. Running it in a browser is undoubtedly convenient, though. Alternatives such as Light Touch offer a fuller implementation, but they demand more than a handy Chrome instance on a Windows device to open a portal back to a brighter time. So, fire up 2006's Nintendo Wii, pop on that CD of Back to Black, and relive the excitement of switching on the very first iPhone. Although perhaps give that other 2007 icon, Windows Vista, a bit of a swerve… ®

9fc10527acaaf794: MIGRANT workers, documented or otherwise, risk exploitation, violence and death just to be in Malaysia.
With nothing to lose and everything to gain — they make a living not just from taking up jobs not fancied by Malaysians, but also by setting up small businesses.

Between 2024 and Sept 30 this year, 25,124 foreigners were detained for illegally running 20 to 23 businesses they could not operate or own, in high-cash and low-barrier-to-entry sectors that form the "shadow economy". Small grocery stores and 24-hour convenience stores selling cheap imported goods are ubiquitous in residential flats, housing estates and commercial hotspots.

Relying on mobility and sidestepping brick-and-mortar investments, migrants sell fresh produce, fruits, garments or cheap electronics at night and farmers' markets, and leverage their cultural and culinary backgrounds to run small coffee shops and restaurants. Operators also use unlicensed, back-alley "cloud kitchens" to supply cuisine all day long.

They also form barber shops and hair salons, automotive maintenance hubs, laundrettes and cleaning services in rented spaces. Meanwhile, some of them run dubious clinics to treat fellow migrants who fear unwanted exposure in public hospitals.
Thanks to "Ali Baba" proxy arrangements with unscrupulous Malaysians, shops can be up and running practically overnight.

The Inland Revenue Board estimates government losses of RM70 billion annually in uncollected taxes from the shadow economy. There are no earnings, personal or corporate, to be declared from this cash-only network.

A stall at the Selayang market or Jalan Silang can pull in an estimated RM20,000 to RM100,000 in monthly revenue. Conversely, legitimate Malaysian small businesses operate on a tight 20 per cent profit margin, so they are bound to be aghast at having to compete against migrant businesses netting as high as 60 per cent margins.
Migrants are able to evade the RM1,850 annual levy, statutory worker contributions and recruitment fees while paying salaries far below the minimum wage.
Profits are immediately remitted to home countries through informal and unmonitored channels that bypass the domestic banking system.
Bank Negara Malaysia estimates that RM32.6 billion is remitted annually, but the Malaysian Employers Federation puts the figure at closer to RM70 billion.

The bigger question is: how do these migrant businesses continue operating despite active enforcement, raids and arrests? The authorities haplessly police every known business premises, but are hampered by non-deterrent penalties that allow migrants to easily reopen under different names.

As long as Malaysians decline dirty, dangerous and demeaning jobs in construction, plantation, manufacturing and domestic work, migrants will fill the void, creating an ecosystem of customers for migrant businesses. The shadow economy thrives because Malaysians are complicit in it.
