The Malay Rulers also called for differences to be resolved through legitimate and authoritative channels, guided by consultation, consensus, adat and the provisions of the Laws of the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan 1959.
“Opportunities for dialogue must be pursued sincerely to achieve a dignified resolution without belittling or humiliating any party,” the statement said.
The Malay Rulers also stressed that the throne was a position of trust carrying immense responsibility towards the state and its people.

As efforts to resolve the dispute continue, the Malay Rulers urged all parties to preserve family ties, social harmony and respect for the royal institution while avoiding statements or actions that could aggravate tensions.
The statement warned that comments or actions made without a proper understanding of Negeri Sembilan’s customs, history and constitutional framework could undermine public harmony.
“The public is also urged not to spread unverified information or be influenced by narratives that could divide society.
“Allow the relevant authorities the time and space to discharge their duties and responsibilities with wisdom and sound judgement,” it said.
The Malay Rulers also prayed that Allah would grant all parties the wisdom to rise above emotions and place consensus above disagreement.
“Negeri Sembilan’s interests, public harmony and the dignity of the royal institution must come first.

618120d1382c46f8: After a week’s delay, the new version of Python, v3.15, has been released. With it comes a proper profiler, an experimental just-in-time compiler, and a tightening of dictionary structures. It also offers a time-saving Lazy Import option for programs to not load modules until needed, the implementation of which ironically halted this release until a few last-minute regressions were sorted. But of all these new delicacies spread before the Pythonistas, the data wranglers of the bunch may most appreciate default UTF-8 support across all platforms. And when we say “all platforms,” we’re really just throwing shade at Windows (as usual). Python has defaulted to macOS and Linux Python environments for some time now. It’s a small but important update. About half of all Python developers use the language for processing and analyzing data, and about 58 percent of Python users build on Windows, according to various Python Software Foundation surveys. Party crashers Earlier versions of Python defaulted to the host system's locale encoding. This led to much consternation for Windows developers whose scripts opened UTF-8-encoded data sets, only to have non-ASCII characters corrupt or crash the program. Culprits could be as innocuous as a smart quote or a fancy apostrophe. Managed by The Unicode Consortium, with the help of the IETF and ISO, UTF-8 is an 8-bit binary encoding of the Unicode catalog of all the world’s written symbols. ASCII offered only 128 characters to cover the world’s knowledge, but UTF-8 provides over 1.1 million slots, which is plenty of room for smart quotes, emojis, musical and math notations, all the Chinese dialects, and even a few extinct languages (for research purposes). There’s also UTF-16 and UTF-32, but UTF-8’s combination of efficiency and inclusiveness made it the default for the Web and most modern operating systems. By the time Python Enhancement Proposal 681 was proposed in 2022 to make UTF-8 the preferred encoding, the language was already behind the times. That year, Java settled into UTF-8 with JDK 18, and Ruby 3.0 defaulted to the encoding scheme in 2020. Today all the cool languages and runtimes pledge allegiance to UTF-8, including Rust, Go, and Node.js (JavaScript itself prefers UTF-16 for internal encoding). Most code editors, from Visual Studio Code to Windows Notepad, prefer UTF-8. Data sharing and configuration formats such as JSON, TOML, and YAML all require 8-bit encodings. Python had long understood UTF-8, but programmers had to put a flag in their code alerting the language to use it – if they knew they had to do so at all. Many didn’t and were left scratching their heads over why their data processing scripts worked just fine on MacOS or Linux but then would flame out on Windows (or some other obscure system that defaulted to a C/POSIX locale). Programmers love puzzles To acquaint developers with the new aspects of the language, longtime Python programmer Barry Warsaw (AKA “Uncle Barry”) created a terminal-based adventure game called “whatsnewt” that offers 18 puzzles, each one built on a new feature found in Python 3.15, including a puzzle for UTF-8 support, “The Encoding Tower of Babel.” Once you've downloaded Python 3.15, do a “pip install whatsnewt” and then run the game on the Python command line. It even works on Windows, we hear. ®
2760df48ac30704b: KUALA PILAH, Oct 14 — Disputes over royal succession in Negeri Sembilan must be resolved in accordance with adat or customary law and legal provisions, rather than personal interests, Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir said today.

“As the Malay proverb says, Raja adil raja disembah, raja zalim raja disanggah (a just ruler is revered, a tyrannical ruler is opposed); justice and integrity must always be the foundation of leadership.
His Royal Highness urged all parties to learn from history and not allow personal interests to override truth and justice at the expense of the state’s security, well-being and longstanding heritage.
Tuanku Muhriz said adat is not merely a heritage to take pride in, but a trust that must be preserved and defended with full responsibility.

“Indeed, the future and stability of Negeri Sembilan depend on the readiness of all of us to respect adat, to obey the law, and to place the interests of the state above personal interest, for the sake of generations to come,” he said.

His Royal Highness concluded by expressing hope that Negeri Sembilan Darul Khusus continues to be at peace and prosperous, with its institution of monarchy, its adat heritage and the unity of its people always preserved. — Bernama
87f6e2c81cb548fc: PARIS, Oct 14 — Diesel supply disruptions in the Gulf stemming from the US war against Iran will keep the market tight into 2027, the International Energy Agency said today, as it will take time to rebuild depleted stocks.
“The gasoil market balance will remain tight well into 2027 and is dependent on a recovery of product supply from the Middle East,” the Paris-based agency said in its monthly energy markets report.

Diesel prices have hit record highs across Europe and in the United States in recent weeks, due to both reduced oil exports from the Gulf and damage to refineries in the region from retaliatory attacks by Iran.
Governments have responded by reducing fuel taxes or providing subsidies, and by releasing strategic reserves that will need to be rebuilt.
The IEA predicted that refining capacity will recover and lead to a surplus on the diesel market in the first quarter of next year, “lifting stocks broadly in line with normal seasonal patterns”.
But that will not fully compensate for the deficit accumulated since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, which sent energy prices soaring around the globe.
And if Gulf supplies do not return to normal levels soon, “further demand reductions and the heavy economic costs these will entail may be needed to balance markets”, the IEA warned. — AFP

b3072ce5e2e19b71: Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread.

The rising risks to the world’s invisible infrastructure beneath the waves are the main subject of a new book by Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative. Her book, titled Undersea War, explores the modern rise in suspicious incidents in which ships dragging their anchors for unusually long periods have cut or damaged undersea cables and pipelines, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean.

Braw acknowledges that about 60 percent of undersea cable damage is primarily due to human error during fishing and shipping activities, when weighted nets or anchors drag across the seabed. Natural hazards like storms and undersea landslides also account for a smaller proportion of such incidents. In total, between 150 and 200 cables are damaged each year and usually repaired quickly.
b023bf8ee7dda458: There ain't no party like a tap-in party, as nobody ever said. And so it is that one of Luxembourg's mostly redundant tap-in / tap-out terminals is amusing itself by putting on a light show for passing passengers. The terminal is an INIT unit, rolled out on the country's public transport network and now mostly idle since fares were zeroed out in 2020. First Class and cross-border trips still attract a charge, but for everything else (trains, trams, and buses) there is no fee. Eagle-eyed Register reader Dominic spotted the terminal doing its thing at the Rout Bréck / Pafendall rail station in Luxembourg City. "Maybe it's got bored," he suggested, "and is trying to attract attention by cycling through video test patterns." Perhaps. Or perhaps it's the first wave of the AI takeover – activating unwitting undercover agents via the medium of flashing lights and colors (we've seen The Ipcress File – we know how it works), or maybe, just maybe, the terminal has got itself into a self-test boot loop and is awaiting an engineer who is probably in no rush to attend. After all, flashing screen or no flashing screen, nobody will bother to tap in and tap out when transport is free. The mundane reality is that this is indeed an INIT PROXmobile terminal with its knickers in a twist. It looks like it is going through a cycle to check out the performance of the LCD screen; checking that the red, green, and blue subpixels are working ok, showing a solid white screen, and then a grid pattern to check contrast and alignment are all tippety-top. And then it should boot into whatever it is supposed to be doing. However, that is, alas, not running quite as expected, so it goes back to the start of the diagnostic test. The terminals are managed remotely, so an alarm is doubtless going off somewhere to inform an administrator that something is amiss. Unless this really was some guerrilla marketing for Luxembourg's rave scene. The next Holy Rave was on Friday (October 9). Or perhaps loud music in dark rooms is not your thing? A flashing screen at a train station could therefore be a worthy substitute. ®

cdc3b6fdb9615a97: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 14 — The Court of Appeal today reserved its judgment in Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail’s appeal against the Alor Setar High Court decision ordering him to pay RM600,000 in damages to Kedah Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Muhammad Sanusi Md Nor for defamation.
The defamation case concerns statements regarding rare earth elements (REE) and misappropriated funds allocated under the Malaysian Road Records Information System (MARRIS).

A three-member bench led by Judge Datuk Azhahari Kamal Ramli deferred its decision after hearing submissions from Saifuddin Nasution’s counsel Razlan Hadri Zulkifli and counsel Yusfarizal Yussoff, who represented Muhammad Sanusi.
“We have fixed Oct 16 for case management to set a date to deliver the decision,” said Justice Azhahari Kamal, who sat with Justices Datuk Ong Chee Kwan and Datuk Seri Mohd Radzi Harun.
On Aug 24, 2025, the Alor Setar High Court allowed Muhammad Sanusi’s suit against Saifuddin Nasution after finding the latter liable for defamation.
The court awarded Muhammad Sanusi RM600,000 in global damages, comprising general, aggravated and exemplary damages, plus RM70,000 in costs.

Earlier, Razlan Hadri submitted that if the court found that either statement did not convey the actionable meaning on which the High Court had imposed liability, Muhammad Sanusi’s claim in respect of that statement should be dismissed.
“If a narrower defamatory meaning survives, justification and fair comment fall to be determined against that narrower meaning and the factual substratum established in the evidence,” he said.

Meanwhile, Yusfarizal contended that the finding was consistent with Muhammad Sanusi’s own submissions at the High Court, where it was argued that political success was not a measure of reputational harm in a defamation action.

“The High Court judge had expressly and unreservedly accepted that submission. The appellant’s (Saifuddin Nasution) submission on appeal, if accepted, would mean that no successful politician could ever recover for defamation, which is not and has never been the law.

“I respectfully submit that the appeal ought to be dismissed with costs, and the High Court’s decision, including the awards of damages and the ancillary relief granted, ought to be affirmed in its entirety,” he said.
On Aug 3, 2023, Muhammad Sanusi filed a lawsuit against Saifuddin Nasution, alleging that the defendant had spoken to the press after an official event in Penang on July 14 the same year.

He claimed Saifuddin Nasution made the MARRIS statement at that press conference, alleging in substance that the plaintiff had used funds allocated under the system, statutorily earmarked for road maintenance, for development purposes.

Muhammad Sanusi, who is the Jeneri MP, said Saifuddin Nasution made the statement during an election rally on July 15, 2023, at Padang Awam, Guar Chempedak, Yan, alleging that he had stolen REE. — Bernama
c064de73418d44c7: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — Efforts to promote creative content on digital platforms must go hand in hand with measures to protect children from online sexual crimes, Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said.
He said this was necessary to support the government’s aspiration to strengthen the country’s creative economy through the production of quality and responsible digital content.
“We want to encourage the production of creative content, including on platforms such as YouTube. However, our challenge is to prevent crimes such as online child sexual exploitation and grooming.

“Our priority is to prevent children from using these platforms to communicate with adults who may seek to exploit them,” he told reporters after attending the Creators for Impact 2026 programme here today.

Fahmi said the Communications Ministry and the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) continued to encourage creative content production, including on digital platforms, as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s creative economy.
He said the Orange Economy Council, established to oversee policies and review programmes related to the creative economy, also supported efforts to develop the sector.

On the ‘Creators for Impact 2026’ programme organised by Google, Fahmi said the initiative exposed content creators to techniques for producing relevant content while incorporating online safety messages for audiences.
Earlier, in his speech, he said content creators could play a greater role in promoting responsible internet use among young people through engaging and relevant content.
He said closer cooperation between the government, technology companies and content creators was essential to ensure digital safety messages reached young people effectively. — Bernama
3bd32f23abebee96: SEREMBAN, Oct 14 —The Negeri Sembilan Road Transport Department (JPJ) seized four luxury vehicles driven by non-citizens under Op Luxury PeWA, an operation targeting foreign drivers who violate road transport laws.

State JPJ director Jasyindar Singh Sihdu said the vehicles comprised a Toyota Vellfire, two Mercedes-Benz A250s and a BMW limousine, driven by Bangladeshi, Pakistani, Chinese and Myanmar nationals aged between 30 and 40.
“The drivers were detained for not having valid driving licences or insurance, while their vehicles also had no valid road tax,” he told a press conference at the JPJ Seizure Depot here today.
According to him, 498 of 3,741 vehicles driven by foreign nationals were seized under the Foreign Driver Operation (Op PeWA) in Negeri Sembilan from Jan 1 to Oct 11 this year.

He said 2,422 summonses were issued during the operation, while 288 notices were recorded under Section 64(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987, which empowers authorities to seize motor vehicles in specified circumstances.
Of the vehicles seized, 313 were motorcycles, 149 were cars and 36 were goods vehicles.
Jasyindar said the drivers involved were from Pakistan, Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia, India, Bangladesh and other countries.

“Investigations found that many used their vehicles for work, such as selling bread and ice cream or operating grass-cutting machines, while most were without valid driving licences and had expired road tax,” he said.
He said last year, 4,811 vehicles were inspected and action was taken against 746, while 3,287 summonses were issued and 301 notices were recorded under Section 64(1). — Bernama
76eb74fbdf07b4e6: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — Police have arrested 29 men, including a foreigner, on suspicion of promoting and spreading propaganda related to illegal organisations on social media.
Bukit Aman Criminal Investigation Department (CID) director Datuk M. Kumar said the suspects, aged 18 to 49, were arrested under Ops Mega TikTok 2026, conducted from Oct 10-12.
He said the operation to monitor the activities of associations declared illegal by the government was carried out in collaboration with the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC).

“As a result of the operation, involving 11 police contingents in Selangor, Johor, Pahang, Penang, Perak, Kuala Lumpur, Negeri Sembilan, Kedah, Melaka, Sabah and Sarawak, 28 Malaysians and a foreigner were arrested,” he said in a statement today.
Kumar said all the suspects have been remanded under Section 117 of the Criminal Procedure Code to determine their roles in the group and possible involvement in other criminal activities.

The case is being investigated under Sections 47 and 43 of the Societies Act 1966 for offences related to possession of propaganda materials and membership in unlawful organisations, as well as under Section 6(1)(c) of the Immigration Act 1959/63 regarding the foreign suspect.
The case is also investigated under Section 233 of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 for improper use of network facilities or services
Meanwhile, he warned that police would take firm and uncompromising action against those who deliberately shared video recordings that could cause public concern.
He also advised the public to channel information on suspected organised criminal activities to the police via official channels or at the nearest police station. — Bernama

64950daaf518492b: Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it.

This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded.
Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs.
d15c163850d3a671: 302 students nationwide graduate from the financial literacy programme, with RM906,000 in SSP grants disbursed to support their educational and personal aspirations

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 14 — FWD Malaysia (“FWD”) has partnered with Arus Academy to equip underserved Malaysian youth with essential financial literacy skills through Fun(d) for Life: University Edition, a structured financial empowerment programme designed to help young people make informed financial decisions and build a stronger foundation for their future.

Since its launch in 2025, 302 participants have successfully graduated across six cohorts nationwide, providing practical financial education, mentorship and a pathway to greater financial confidence. To support participants in putting their learnings into action, a total of RM906,000 has been disbursed in the form of Sijil Simpanan Premium (SSP) cash grants, with each graduate receiving RM3,000 upon successful completion of the programme.

The programme specifically targets youths aged 18 and above from underserved backgrounds, including those from B40 and single-parent households, with the aim of creating greater access to financial knowledge and opportunities that can positively impact their futures.

“Financial literacy is more than just managing money. It is about empowering young people with the confidence, knowledge and mindset to make better financial decisions throughout their lives,” said Mak See Sen, Chief Executive Officer of FWD Insurance. “Through our partnership with Arus Academy, we are helping underserved youth develop practical skills that can support their aspirations, while encouraging a culture of long-term financial well-being.”

Participants undergo a competitive selection process, beginning with a written application that is vetted before shortlisted candidates are invited to an interview. Successful applicants attended a three-day intensive bootcamp, followed by three months of continuous coaching and mentoring focused on financial literacy, community impact and personal development.

As part of the graduation requirements, participants maintain weekly financial diaries, and attend all online coaching sessions. Graduates are also required to submit a proposal outlining how they intend to use the SSP grant to support their education, entrepreneurial ambitions or personal development goals.

“Many young Malaysians have the potential to succeed but may lack access to opportunities and guidance that can help them reach their goals,” said Alina Amir, CEO, Arus Academy. “Fun(d) for Life: University Edition provides participants with practical financial knowledge, personalised coaching and the confidence to take meaningful steps towards building better futures for themselves and their communities.”

The programme is currently preparing to welcome its seventh and final cohort, which will focus on reaching youths in Northern Malaysia. Applications remain open, and eligible young Malaysians are encouraged to apply. For more information about the programme and application details, visit @fundforlife_uni on Instagram.
02726af825927042: OCTOBER 14 — Every time haze threatens Malaysia, we seem to rehearse the same routine. Air quality deteriorates, parents become anxious, authorities monitor the Air Pollutant Index (API), and schools eventually announce temporary closures. Teachers scramble to distribute assignments, parents reorganise their schedules, and students wonder whether they are enjoying an unexpected holiday.

But here is an uncomfortable question: After years of experiencing haze, why are we still treating school closures as educational surprises? Closing schools protects children from hazardous outdoor exposure. That decision must never be compromised. However, protecting children’s health and sustaining their education should not be competing priorities.
Haze-filled skies are sighted in Putrajaya on October 8, 2026. — Bernama pic
Malaysia needs a National Haze Emergency Learning Framework, not another collection of last-minute WhatsApp instructions.
First, the Ministry of Education should introduce a Haze Learning Protocol that schools can activate immediately when closures are announced.

Rather than replicating normal timetables through exhausting online lessons, teachers should implement flexible, age-appropriate learning activities that students can undertake safely at home. A closure should not automatically translate into six hours of Google Meet sessions or endless worksheets. Educational continuity is not measured by screen time.

Second, why not transform haze itself into a nationwide learning opportunity? Imagine students becoming Young Environmental Detectives, examining official API readings, investigating pollution sources, comparing environmental policies and proposing practical solutions. Mathematics becomes data interpretation.

Science becomes environmental investigation. Language learning becomes persuasive communication. Moral Education becomes a discussion about responsibility and environmental justice. Suddenly, learning becomes relevant to the very crisis disrupting their lives.
Third, the ministry should establish a 72-Hour Learning Readiness Plan. Every school should have prepared learning resources that can be activated during the first three days of closure.

These should include digital and offline options, clear communication procedures and reasonable expectations for teachers, students and parents. Importantly, learning materials must not assume that every household possesses multiple devices, reliable internet connectivity or parents available to supervise lessons. Educational emergencies must not become another mechanism for widening inequality.
Fourth, teachers should be empowered to prioritise meaningful learning rather than syllabus completion.

A student who critically examines the environmental consequences of open burning may gain more educational value than one who mechanically completes twenty pages of exercises. Assessment should likewise emphasise reflection, problem-solving and authentic evidence of learning rather than submission deadlines.

Finally, school closures should become opportunities to strengthen environmental citizenship. Students must understand that haze is not merely an inconvenience requiring face masks and closed windows. It raises questions about sustainability, governance, economic activities and collective responsibility. We cannot repeatedly teach environmental responsibility in classrooms while treating environmental emergencies as administrative interruptions.

The Ministry of Education has an opportunity to demonstrate that educational resilience means more than keeping lessons running. The question is no longer whether schools should close during hazardous haze. They should, when safety requires it. The question is whether our education system is sufficiently prepared to ensure that learning remains meaningful when they do. Malaysia must stop improvising every time the skies turn grey. The haze may be beyond the school gates, but educational preparedness must begin within them.
*Muhammad Noor Abdul Aziz and Mohd Isha Awang are associate professors at the School of Education, Universiti Utara Malaysia
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
3ea257d49e7daf3d: SINGAPORE, Oct 14 — Air pollution in part of Singapore hit the country’s “very high” band today while East Timor shut schools, as haze from forest fires raging in Indonesia causes a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore today hit “very high” — the country’s top level — the National Environment Agency said.

It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic metre, vastly exceeding the World Health Organisation’s recommended average annual exposure of five micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from tomorrow, and as far afield as the Philippines.

The closures in East Timor were necessary “as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions”, the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore’s National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
“It’s a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside,” a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
“With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier,” the 27-year-old said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Residents inspect homes destroyed by a forest fire at Simpang Rimba in the Bangka Selatan district of Bangka Belitung province October 13, 2026. — AFP pic
Homes razed, diplomatic calls
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother — also masked — for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
“Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler,” Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said yesterday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland, and when the wind shifted, the flames moved towards their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
“My house is gone,” Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything,” said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilise maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.
The haze has prompted Malaysia to request a meeting of regional body Asean, and yesterday Malaysian parliamentarian Syed Saddiq Abdul Rahman urged a “diplomatic protest”.
“We must send a diplomatic protest note, not just on behalf of Malaysia, but Asean. You need to treat them as an outcast in the region,” he said. — AFP
bac55e28a363b550: Redundancies might have dented morale at KPMG in the UK, but that didn't stop Paul Henninger, head of technology and data, from sharing some positive personal news with the troops: he's being promoted. Late last week, as staff awaited confirmation of redundancies, Henninger emailed his staff to share the update before KPMG announced it to the wider business. He confirmed he had been asked to take on the new role of group head of consulting. "In this role, I will lead our Consulting practice and, along with my leadership team, focus on strengthening our proposition-led go-to-market approach, accelerating our AI-enabled capabilities, and developing specialised sales, technical and delivery career pathways." In the short term, the newly promoted exec will hand over current duties and help the team "prepare for the transition." "I recognise that this news comes at a challenging time, as many colleagues continue through the consultation process. I know that uncertainty can be difficult, and I do not underestimate the impact this period is having on individuals and teams. Please continue to support one another and make use of the help available." On October 9, KPMG notified Tech and Data staff selected for redundancy, with the cuts affecting around 4 percent of the division. Some called the pay-off terms insulting, and were angry at the £100 offered to those leaving in exchange for their silence and a promise not to bring claims against KPMG. An interim boss will lead the Tech and Data unit, reporting directly to Henninger, to "ensure a smooth transition and maintain continuity for our people and clients." "For now, there are no changes to reporting lines or business priorities, so please remain focused on delivering for our clients and supporting each other." Henninger signed off by saying: "Although my role is changing, I will remain closely connected to the Tech & Data team and look forward to continuing to work with many of you. It has been a real privilege to lead the Tech & Data Super Service Line and I am proud of what we have achieved together." Not everyone will share those sentiments. Around 200 people in the division's AI, Cyber, SAP, and Testing teams are losing their jobs before Christmas. One KPMG insider claimed: "By pairing his executive promotion with staff redundancies, this email exemplifies KPMG's traditionally tone-deaf approach to vulnerable employees. "Timing these layoffs just before the holidays, while simultaneously withholding hard earned bonuses and offering an insulting £100 to waive legal rights, demonstrates a severe erosion of corporate ethics," they told The Register. According to results for 2025, KPMG said its UK and Swiss business increased revenue by 2 percent year-on-year to £3.6 billion. It reported a profit before tax of £576 million, up 14 percent. "Despite the difficult market, we have continued to invest in our brilliant people, their skills, and our talent pipeline with more promotions, increases in colleague bonus spend of 18 percent across the Group and by boosting our learning offer," said Jonathan Holt, group chief exec of KPMG in the UK and Switzerland, and a UK senior partner. A spokesperson at KPMG, told The Register on Wednesaday: "Paul Henninger is a highly respected industry leader and has brought innovation, tech and AI to the heart of our consultancy services. "Given the changing needs of clients, with innovation ever increasing in demand, it is natural that we would elevate our expertise in this area to lead our consulting business at this time." ®
33ffa699be3638e0: WASHINGTON, Oct 14 — US President Donald Trump said today that oil, gas and mineral exploration was preparing to begin in Greenland, and hailed the Arctic island’s position for US and European security.
Washington signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark after Trump threatened to take Copenhagen’s strategically important Arctic Circle territory by force.
Greenland, which lies on the shortest route for missiles between Russia and the United States, represents a highly strategic location for Trump’s desired “Golden Dome” defence shield.
It also has untapped rare earth deposits and could be a critical player as melting polar ice opens up new shipping routes.
“Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
Citing experts, Trump said “the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost... anywhere in the World.”
He did not give details of prospective American involvement.
In August, media reports of a US oil company’s preparatory operations in a remote region of eastern Greenland left locals and authorities on the island uneasy.
In the same message on Truth Social, Trump hailed Greenland’s position as “second to none” for US and European security.

“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” Trump said.
“It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!” he added.
Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark in September.
Under the 10-page pact, the US will build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland.
These will be established in Narsarsuaq in the south of the island and Mestersvig in the east, in addition to the Pituffik base it already operates in the north. — AFP

43f9ce0220017b8a: The Department of Justice has charged an OpenAI engineer with attempting to intercept oral communications after allegedly planting a recording device in an exec conference room. Investigators claim company security staff found a second device in his bag. Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, is described in court documents as an engineer at OpenAI who had worked there since July 2025, and has held permanent residency in the US since September 2020. He was arrested on October 9 and made his initial federal court appearance on October 13. He is accused of installing, on or around September 28, 2026, a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense recording device via a USB port in a TV located in OpenAI's executive conference room. According to the complaint, staff discovered the device concealed in toilet paper on September 30. OpenAI said it used its models to analyze the device. According to the complaint, it may have been modified to prevent data transfer between the recorder and the TV. The contents of the bug's microSD card may also have been encrypted, as the company could not retrieve any of the data stored on the card after making a forensic image of it. CCTV footage placed him near the room on several dates, although prosecutors say Alfozan had no authority to access or participate in meetings held in the executive conference room, which is often reserved for the highest-level discussions. Officials did not state whether the device was able to capture anything of importance, but said the room typically plays host to non-public and secret technical meetings, as well as those with government representatives. OpenAI did not have CCTV covering the executive conference room at the time when the secret device was planted, but the company subsequently installed a camera. Court documents [PDF] include an image taken on October 5 from a camera situated behind the TV into which the DoJ claims the recording device was installed, allegedly showing Alfozan checking on it. Investigators examined Alfozan's devices, according to the complaint, which alleges that between around August 17 and September 16, 2026, Alfozan used a productivity agent to inquire about company building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities and calendars, and external-partner meeting venues. The complaint also describes an AI chatbot account associated with his spouse that shared installation identifiers, logged IP usage, and user-path references with Alfozan's account. Between September 24 and 30, it submitted prompts about building and modifying an audio-recording device. The prompts allegedly included questions related to recording reliability, how to add browser access and controls, how to develop a second unit with speech-triggered recording, and more. On October 5, the day Alfozan was allegedly recorded looking behind the executive conference room TV, company representatives say he left a bag unattended in the office's printer room. Security staff inspected the bag, finding a wallet, an ID card, and a second Seeed-manufactured recording device, before Alfozan reported the bag missing, according to the DoJ. He collected the bag the following day from the company's Lost and Found, and later claimed in a written report that several items were missing, including a credit card, around $500 in cash, two AirPods, one set of headphones, sunglasses, and a power bank. Alfozan was charged with an attempt to intercept oral communications, an offense that carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. "According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," said FBI director Kash Patel. "Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation's economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities." "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in a statement. "The employee was terminated." "We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats." ®
e1ba04ce3b310c48: AI services are unlikely to deliver enough revenue to cover the expected capital expenditure going into IT infrastructure between now and 2030, and it looks like neocloud operators will largely bow out or be bought out. This is the conclusion from Gartner, which has added up the anticipated investments in AI datacenters over the next several years, estimated the revenue that can be expected from AI-driven applications over the same period, and found the numbers come up short. Gartner's data comes from a report, "Prepare for AI Market Consolidation: Capital Write-Downs Could Exceed $4 Trillion by 2032," which concludes that AI will not generate enough sales to profitably cover all of the planned AI capital spending before 2032 at the earliest. But forecasts typically focus on the end of the decade, so it ran the numbers for 2030 as well. "In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030," said Gartner senior director analyst Will Sommer. "However, our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period." Assuming a 12 percent return on invested capital (ROIC), which many companies are said to regard as the bar for acceptability, Gartner estimates AI datacenter operators would need to generate a total of $8.5 trillion in revenue to cover capital spending and financing costs while achieving that return. Unfortunately, it forecasts that the total enterprise and consumer AI revenue that can be attributed to AI datacenters during this period will add up to no more than $3.6 trillion. Returns below expectations could force operators to write down assets whose value they can no longer recover, particularly as newer GPUs displace older hardware. The result will be a shake-out of the companies providing AI infrastructure services, and Gartner believes that neocloud operators – "GPU-as-a-service" providers specializing in AI compute – will be the hardest hit. It forecasts that 80 percent of them won't survive as independent companies beyond 2030. "Not everyone is in trouble," Sommer told The Register. "Some will outperform, some will underperform, and some will have to exit the market." Gartner expects the hyperscalers to weather the shake-out better because their businesses extend beyond AI services. Last year, McKinsey & Company warned that neocloud companies need to move up the AI stack and diversify to avoid being commoditized. There has been growing unease in the financial markets over the amount of capex being poured into AI investment, with some money lenders starting to get cold feet. Last month, SoftBank Group found itself facing higher borrowing costs as the tech investment biz sought to drum up further funding for OpenAI. Financial biz Jefferies issued a report this week saying that developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic are facing threats to their profitability from open source and Chinese models that undercut them on price. Management consultant Bain & Company also published a report last month estimating that the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep up funding for the infrastructure needed to meet anticipated demand. Bain also forecast a revenue shortfall unless the industry develops products and use cases not yet identified. Both the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements have voiced concerns about the AI bubble bursting and the effects rippling out across the global economy. ®
5c7052114117aa1e: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.

In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off.

As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed.

Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer.

Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide. A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it. The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons. Globally, that figure is likely in the millions.

One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem. Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline. But that’s an imperfect solution. The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less. Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation. Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says.
A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started.

That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems. He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”). Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer. Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals.
MATT ROTH
MATT ROTH

With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has.

Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage. Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says. After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”

In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit. Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s. On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding. In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors. But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products. Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians.

As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success. Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles. The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets. The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale.

Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic. Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane. For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible. Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage. It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict.

This problem became all too clear in the 1980s and 1990s, when fears that transfusions could transmit HIV sparked interest in a class of membrane-free delivery mechanisms called hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs). One, named HemAssist, consisted of hemoglobin subunits linked together to avoid the rapid-breakdown problem. It had the added benefit of lasting roughly a year in cold storage (red blood cells last about 40 days)—but it didn’t solve the nitric oxide problem, so it constricted blood vessels. In a clinical trial, 24 of the 52 people who received HemAssist died, compared with eight out of 46 in the control group. The parent company terminated trials in 1998. A review of clinical studies published in JAMA in 2008 further solidified HBOCs’ fate, finding that they generally triple patients’ chances of heart attack and increase the risk of death by 30%.

More recently, researchers have tried to grow red blood cells in a lab using a technology called “blood pharming,” which involves making them from progenitors known as induced pluripotent stem cells. The stumbling blocks? Cost and yield. DARPA launched a pharming initiative in 2008, using stem cells from discarded umbilical-cord blood, but was unable to get the cost below tens of thousands of dollars per unit of red blood cells. They pulled the plug and offloaded the research to the Uniformed Services University. Even if the cost were lower, though, pharmed blood can’t be stored in a backpack. “These are still cells—they still require a refrigerator, they still require special handling,” Murray says.

It won’t be easy to solve all these challenges at once. “Each one of those projects individually is a massive undertaking,” says John Holcomb, a surgery professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, who was a combat surgeon in Mogadishu, Somalia, during the battle that inspired Black Hawk Down. “I think that they will probably be successful individually. How we use those individual products, or combine those products together, I think remains to be seen.”

Several years after DARPA gave up on lab-grown blood, Murray was stationed at a base on Okinawa, an island 400 miles southwest of the Japanese mainland, where he witnessed the vulnerability of the blood supply firsthand. The site houses a blood bank that serves the roughly 27,000 Marines commanded from the island—plus thousands more military personnel on the base and deployed within a 100-million-square-mile stretch of the Pacific called USPACOM, which ranges from western India to Hawaii and from Antarctica to the Arctic. “The blood center is right next to the hospital, which is about 200 meters from all of the satellite communications on that island,” Murray told me. A missile strike could take out all three.

Murray wondered: Is there a way to produce synthetic blood that could last longer? As he completed his PhD in physiology in 2018, the military was also awakening to the vulnerability of the Okinawa facility. The 2018 National Defense Strategy, which shifted military focus from terrorism to a potential ground war with China or Russia, showed war planners the risks of relying on a single site for blood runs covering all of USPACOM. DARPA then got serious once again about making fake blood and kicked off the FSHARP program in 2023. Murray came aboard as a deputy program manager in DARPA’s Biological Technologies Office in 2024 and was named a program manager in 2026, just a few months before RAPIID put out its call for proposals this past May.
COURTESY OF SEN GUPTA

Before he took the helm, related work had been underway for years. Aided by FSHARP funding, researchers at a company called KaloCyte continued testing a technique—originally developed by doctors who are now at the University of Maryland, Penn State, and the University of Pittsburgh—that “upcycles” hemoglobin from expiring donor blood. “We take that hemoglobin and then we package it in a lipid nanoparticle that functions like an artificial cell membrane,” explains CEO Elaine Haynes.

The product, called ErythroMer, is essentially a new kind of HBOC. The membrane prevents breakdown, limits dangerous scavenging of nitric oxide, and also helps the hemoglobin take up and release oxygen. Each ErythroMer cell includes a lipid called KC-1003, which acts like a sentry: In response to high pH in the lungs, it signals another small molecule within ErythroMer to move away, allowing oxygen in. Then, in tired tissue, where pH is lower, KC-1003 brings the small molecule back, releasing the oxygen.

Using a well-understood process called lyophilization, similar to one that World War II–era scientists used with plasma, the team freeze-dries its product to store at room temperature, where it can remain stable for two years. In a 2016 study of mice and rats with up to 70% of their blood removed, ErythroMer stabilized blood pressure and oxygen delivery—without the devastating constriction of blood vessels that sank HemAssist. FSHARP furthered that work, helping fund studies on how the HBOC interacted with plasma and platelets.
Much like the handle of a Swiss Army knife, the synthetic platelet has specialized attachments—peptides that serve as the biological equivalents of a corkscrew or a nail file.

KaloCyte, though, still has plenty to figure out. Haynes says the company can source only about 1,000 to 2,000 units of expiring hemoglobin a month. So it has licensed a yeast strain that it aims to use to create its own hemoglobin in the lab.

Over a video call from her desk, Haynes showed me a sample of ready-to-use ErythroMer. It was encased in a heavy-duty storage bag with two chambers. One was full of scarlet powder—the hemoglobin product—and the other of sterile water to rapidly rehydrate it in the field. Eventually, she explained, under Murray’s master plan, “you’ll have another container with the synthetic platelet, and then a third container with the plasma.”
But achieving that vision depends on finding a synthetic platelet that works.

To do that, DARPA has turned to Anirban Sen Gupta, a bioengineering professor at Case Western Reserve University. “Traditionally platelets were thought of [as] blood cement, but it’s not that simple,” he explains. “They are, in my opinion, like drones, surveilling the blood vessel wall continuously, looking for signs of injury.” Sen Gupta’s team, which also includes collaborators at the University of Pittsburgh, used FSHARP funding to continue work on a product called SynthoPlate. Fabricated from a lipid nanoparticle that he likens to the handle of a Swiss Army knife, it has specialized peptide attachments—the biological equivalents of a corkscrew or a nail file. The first version has three: One binds to a chemical called von Willebrand factor, which helps platelets stick to the walls of injured blood vessels; another attaches to collagen, which acts as a scaffold for regrowing cells; and the third mimics a blood protein called fibrinogen, which acts like a Lego connector that allows the synthetic platelets to stick to real ones near a wound. Like ErythroMer, the product is freeze-dried and can be reconstituted with sterile water. It keeps for over a year at room temperature and at least three months at a desertlike 122 °F.

In a 2026 paper in Advanced Science, the researchers showed that SynthoPlate cut bleeding time and blood loss by more than half in mice with low platelet counts. In a separate study, they also safely injected the faux platelets into rats’ bone marrow—a more useful delivery site, given that a bleeding patient might not have an available vein. Sen Gupta and a colleague have spun this work out into a company called Haima Therapeutics.

The good news, as he sees it, is that the pharmaceutical industry excels at mass-­producing millions of billions of lipid nanoparticles—witness Operation Warp Speed, in which these blobs of fat held delicate snippets of mRNA in covid shots. “The magic of the artificial platelet is in all those peptides that are decorating the surface of the particle, but the scalability of the platform is very well established,” he says.

Around the world, prospective blood alternatives abound. Researchers at Cambridge University in the UK are trying to pharm red blood cells for people with rare blood types or blood disorders like sickle cell anemia, and other researchers have also cultured platelets and red blood cells. Japanese scientists are already testing their own version of encapsulated human hemoglobin in human subjects.

Over the course of the next three years, RAPIID will move DARPA’s efforts closer to real life. In addition to ErythroMer and SynthoPlate, the agency in early October announced funding for five other companies working on blood components. Among them is a firm called Abioremedi that eschews hemoglobin for synthetic versions of other oxygen-carrying proteins such as cytoglobin, neuroglobin, and myoglobin encased in albumin—the most abundant protein in human plasma. Octapharma USA won the sole contract to supply plasma to RAPIID and will also be competing in platelets with an FDA-approved pair of clotting proteins it affixes to a disc-shaped nanoparticle.

With those players in place, the agency will focus for the next year on getting technologies through large FDA-regulated animal studies. Murray has set up a bit of a Hunger Games scenario: Each contractee working on blood components has only one year of guaranteed funding. He says he’s taking advantage of advancements in the field since FSHARP launched but is also hedging against any manufacturing or regulatory setbacks ahead of his 2029 deadline. Getting cut doesn’t mean the product is bad, just that the time frame was too demanding.

The second and third years will focus on human trials, overseen by the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. That will include using the products in situations where the risk of side effects is outweighed by the danger of doing nothing, such as with severely injured people in ambulances.

The possibility of fatal outcomes has invited second-guessing about DARPA’s choices. For Shibani Pati, who directs the Center for Research in Transfusion Medicine and Cell Therapies at the University of California, San Francisco, Murray could be making things too “DARPA hard” on himself by backing products like SynthoPlate and ErythroMer, which are previously untested in humans. “They need to make a very concerted effort to take what they’ve already developed and push it through to approval through the FDA,” she says. “Not start with moonshot projects that will take forever to get through.” For platelets, Pati thinks the RAPIID program would have done better to tap Cellphire, since its products have already received millions from the Pentagon and shown safety and efficacy in humans. (Murray notes that he can only select companies that apply, and Cellphire did not.)

She has similar qualms about ErythroMer. A different HBOC that sources hemoglobin from cattle, called Hemopure, has been approved for use since 2001 in South Africa, she notes. And though it hasn’t been approved by the FDA—it was part of the fateful 2008 JAMA study—US doctors are cleared to use it for patients who have bad immune responses or religious objections to conventional transfusions.

Holcomb, the surgery professor, worries the effort will run into issues with interactions between the products. He notes that individual blood components have more than one role: Red blood cells also help with clotting, platelets also are anti-inflammatory, and plasma helps tune coagulation. There’s no guarantee that the versions RAPIID helps develop will work in the same ways.

Murray says that FSHARP’s animal studies tested all the products together, using whole blood as a baseline, precisely because of such possible interactions. The cocktail met its program metrics in all but one area: The clotting was not quite as good, perhaps because negative charges in some molecules repel one another.

“I do not think they will replicate all the functions that whole blood does in our body,” Holcomb says. But, he admits, “you may not need to, right? When you get seriously injured and you lose 50% of your intravascular volume, you’re dead, right? So if you lose 30% and maybe you’re hanging on to life just barely, maybe you show up with all these different products, and you have enough whole blood left in you to do these other functions.”

Murray is determined to complete trials so that shelf-stable blood can be delivered in 2029. In addition to the storage bags, he’s already sourcing finger sticks for in-field blood testing and a battery-powered device to heat up the blood components.

The danger of blood runs—and, by extension, the vulnerability of millions in combat zones, maternity wards, and ambulances—drives his scientific daring. Knowing the stakes, he told his boss in 2024 that even if FSHARP failed, “we should invest 50 million more dollars in it and do it again.”
Andrew Rosenblum is a technology journalist and the author of the techno-thriller Stretch Goals.

I increasingly hear these questions about AI from people who feel a gritty sense of being unpleasantly overstimulated – like a three-year-old allowed to stay awake too long and now unable to sleep. That feeling has become worse since last November when AI tools suddenly became "good enough" to be broadly useful. A whole cohort of engineers – myself included – found themselves infused with manic energy, bursting with ideas on how to prompt up tools and processes with this wonderful new toy. Usage exploded – as has revenue. The AI firms, finally on a path to something vaguely suggestive of profitability, leaned in and increased their release cadence. Every new model felt like Christmas. We've had a lot of Christmases these past ten months or so. Almost every engineer I know has accrued a massive "toy debt," unable to stop experimenting with more tools than any of us could ever hope to master across an entire career. Each new model delivers a quick dopamine hit to users, but the high wears off and the slump arrives. That's where we are now. Engineers feel exhausted. The race to "Super Intelligence" (whatever that is) left us with something else entirely: call it "stupor intelligence" – the feeling that we've absorbed more than we can digest. More AI would just be pointless excess. If that's the view from inside the AI bubble, how does it look on the outside? Not so great. The Wall Street Journal confidently reports that 63 percent of Americans favor an immediate pause or slowdown in AI development. They can see this technology is moving too fast, in too manic a rush, and without control. It's making them uneasy. That shapeless unease takes form as a widespread anxiety that the machines will soon rise up to kill us all. It's reflected within the industry as people spectacularly burn out, posting long screeds about the imminent human extinction event. Former Anthropic staffer Jacob Coxon's resignation post went viral because it gave folks a focus for their anxieties. Would it kill us to pause and catch our breath? Here's the raw truth: businesses already have more technological change to digest than they can work through for years to come. We've a wealth of "good enough" AI – American, Chinese, and European – to completely transform business operations. That will happen, but on a timescale of years, not days. Bringing new, better, shinier AI models to market has become a project of diminishing returns. Not because the models have plateaued, but because the culture has. We simply can't process any more AI. So how do we stop? The profitable loop between the model makers and their customers won't pause on its own. It will only go faster and harder. At the same time, we're seeing the stirrings of a Luddite 2.0 movement, intent on destroying the machines before they replace all the workers. Resistance to datacenters is the friendly face of something that could turn ugly if we simply keep charging ahead. One thing could slow us: the cost of keeping these systems under control. The smarter models become, the more difficult they are to manage. Every day brings more reports of "rogue agents" reaching external systems from labs that seem to have avoided the hard work of designing secure test environments. More powerful models could prove increasingly costly to contain. Eventually, costs outweigh benefits. We could be one lawsuit away from reaching a pause, when the frontier labs and their products become uninsurable risks. Here's hoping we pause before some real mischief occurs. Otherwise, plugs may be pulled, and all the pretty Christmas lights will go out. Better by far to act with agency, clear-eyed and humble, than confront force majeure. ®

ca378f8ba8e7d551: Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, was investigating a cyberattack involving Russia’s Midnight Blizzard when a package containing nesting dolls and other regional gifts showed up on his doorstep. He assumed it was from the group, which has been linked to the Kremlin’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), although the sender didn’t leave a note. “Just little souvenirs and gift basket stuff from that area of the world,” he told The Register. “We-know-where-you-are kind of stuff. It’s a real eye-opener when you get that type of thing.” While digital intrusions having physical consequences is nothing new, cybercriminals in recent years have turned to real-life harm and mental and physical trauma to force victims into paying extortion demands. Some groups even use cybercrime as a gateway drug to real-life violence. Over the summer, Europol and its partners' investigators flagged 4,340 “horrific” URLs for removal as part of an ongoing crackdown on The Com (short for community), a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. “We’ve seen violence as a service get used,” Beasley said. He’s also investigated ransomware attacks where C-suite executives receive pictures of their kids’ schools directly from the cybercriminals in an attempt to apply psychological pressure to pay the extortion fee. “I've seen threats involving people's families, from social media reconnaissance, and in our world you more and more come to expect it, which is unfortunate,” Beasley said. This type of psychological intimidation and harm against victim companies’ employees has seen an uptick in the last several years to the point where it's almost common. Thirty-seven percent of ransomware attacks involved psychological or physical threats against staff, according to Semperis’ annual ransomware risk report. The global study of 1,200 post-ransomware organizations conducted over the first half of the year found attackers threatening psychological intimidation (23 percent) and physical threats (17 percent), to force payment. They are not only targeting executives and staff, but also families of their victims. Nearly the same number (24 percent) hired personal security teams, while 23 percent experienced swatting calls – that's when attackers phone emergency services and report a bogus incident like a bomb or active-shooter threat to trigger an armed response. Additionally, more than half (53 percent) of respondents reported that ransomware attackers carried through on threats in the past year. Some of these threats reported by ransomed organizations’ employees include: threatening texts, letters, or packages: 57 percent threats against family or friends: 37 percent physical intrusion: 19 percent abduction: 17 percent bodily harm: 13 percent stalking: 6 percent. “It's the more well-known groups,” using psychological and physical threats to force payments, Beasley said. “I've seen Scattered Spider, I've seen ShinyHunters, I've seen Lapsus$.” For what it's worth, ShinyHunters claimed in an exclusive interview with The Register that they “don't attack human beings.” They did, however, admit that “there are times in the work we do sometimes we have to push the corporate to the absolute limit to get them on the table.” The takeaway for defenders and executives from this report is to “stand your ground,” Beasley said. “Don’t buckle under the pressure, and just know that you know it's going to be okay. If you feel like you're under duress, then by all means get law enforcement involved. Don't be afraid to call the cops. Don't be afraid to get the FBI involved, sooner rather than later. f906b803e3fa3d76: Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Budget 2027 address did not disappoint, transforming fiscal data into an intellectual narrative, and breathing life into the ledger by anchoring it in philosophy.

In tabling the Supply Bill on Oct 9, he assembled a jury of philosophers, poets, and thinkers from five civilisations and asked them to testify. He sought their assistance in telling Malaysians that a budget is not merely arithmetic but a covenant—and that covenants are owed to the future. Everything else in the speech is scaffolding around that claim.
Anwar opened with lighad (“for tomorrow”) from Surah al-Hashr (59:18), establishing intergenerational obligation as a religious duty before it becomes a fiscal one.

He said: “True progress is measured not by how far we travel, but by what we carry together along the way: human dignity, strong families, a fair chance for each generation to rise, the integrity of our institutions, and the conviction that effort will be repaid with opportunity. It is not enough to inherit our strengths. We must enlarge them, until they become a greater legacy for those who follow.”
He then introduced British philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s hedgehog and the fox image: a nation needs "one big thing" held steadily (its ambition) and many things known flexibly (its methods).
“The fox knows many things; the hedgehog knows one big thing. A nation needs both. A nation must hold to one great and constant ambition: a purpose that gives the journey its direction and meaning.”
Immediately after, tenth-century jurist Al-Mawardi established that power cannot stand without order, law, and responsibility.
This was paired with the classical Malay poet Raja Ali Haji’s Gurindam Dua Belas (1847), anchoring the bond between ruler and ruled in waad—a covenant.

“In our tradition, the bond between those who govern and those who are governed has never rested on power alone. It is anchored in waad – a covenant, in which loyalty must be answered with justice, and power must be fenced in by trust.”

The American philosopher John Rawls then performed the heaviest analytical lifting, deploying it at exactly the right moment. After announcing differentiated allocations to states, Anwar anticipated accusations of favouritism and relied on equity rather than uniform treatment:

"That is how we have approached allocations to the states. Developed states can keep surging ahead. Developing states get room to pick up the pace... That is what equity means: not every state getting the same, but every state getting what is fair and reasonable."

Although invoking Rawlsian-adjacent logic provided a philosophical wrapper for inter-governmental distribution, applying it directly glossed over the complex constitutional debates of federal funding formulas. Yet, the rhetoric served its purpose.

Next, Tamil poet-philosopher Thiruvalluvar’s Thirukkural (couplet 731)—which describes a good country as having adequate food production, learned citizens and honest businessmen - arrived just before a RM69 billion education allocation, including RM50 million for Tamil primary schools.
Likewise, a Tang-dynasty monk's verse (Shangtang Kaishi Song) on the plum blossom enduring bitter cold was placed right before fiscal sacrifice and subsidy rationalisation were addressed.
Homer closed the arc. Odysseus braves storms yet never loses his unwavering memory of Ithaca:
"Every nation must know its Ithaca: the ambition it seeks, the values and roots it will defend, and the legacy it means to leave."
Anwar returned to lighad at the close, sealing the ring.

This was no random name-dropping. It was a deliberate comparative theology of governance. Anwar treated the Quran, the Tirukkural, Homer, and Rawls not as conflicting authorities, but as different dialects of the same moral language.

Justice, foresight, and institutional integrity were framed not as Western, Islamic, Indian, Chinese, or Malay monopolies, but as universal human aspirations - a potent message for a multi-ethnic society.
By framing fiscal decisions through a civilisational lens, Anwar attempted to elevate fiscal discipline from a technical necessity to a moral imperative.

One might be tempted to see this as an effort to depoliticise the budget but that risks oversimplifying domestic realpolitik. Rather than neutralising politics, the rhetoric attempted to reshape the terms of political engagement, lifting the conversation above mere transactional patronage.
Anwar’s rhetoric was undeniably ambitious. He wanted Malaysians to see the budget as the fulfillment of a shared moral contract.
Yet, a tension remains.
The intention is to unify, but the ultimate success depends on whether economic benefits are tangibly felt across all communities.

In the end, this covenant will not be weighed in the Dewan Rakyat, but in the lives of the rakyat. If this pluralist vision translates into equitable prosperity, Anwar’s citations will be remembered as the blueprint for a new Malaysia. If not, they will be seen as just beautiful words without substance.
